items.title: A single inference process underlies the behavior and neural circuits of working memory
items.content: arXiv:2611.22054v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Working memory holds past inputs online for future behavior. Despite decades of research, accounts of working memory remain divided across levels of analysis, with long-standing debates on whether its capacity reflects discrete slots or continuous resources, how attention improves recall, and whether its representations rely on persistent neural firing or activity-silent states. Here we show that MemGP, a theory that is specified at the computational, algorithmic, and circuit levels of analysis simultaneously, can explain diverse behavioral and neural phenomena in working memory. At the computational level, MemGP casts working memory as probabilistic inference over a continuous function on feature space, with a variational objective that balances memory strength against a Gaussian-process prior. At the algorithmic level, writing, storing, and reading of memories correspond to approximating this posterior with a finite set of inducing points, the resource that all items share. In simulations, MemGP reproduces load-dependent precision loss, attentional benefits during maintenance, and inter-item attraction and repulsion, in each case revealing multiple complex computational dependencies. At the circuit level, the algorithm analytically (without training) maps onto a recurrent circuit, including its architecture and dynamics. Beyond reproducing neural phenomena such as delay-dependent drift, this analytical map deduces center--surround connectivity, a property long assumed in attractor models, and a structured combination of persistent activity and synaptic weights to hold memories. Thus, a single inference objective not only jointly predicts the behavioral and neural signatures of working memory, but also addresses, across several instances and different levels of analysis, existing competing explanations.

items.title: CrisisBench: an evaluation suite for crisis counseling AI
items.content: arXiv:2611.21622v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Background: Crisis helplines are essential to mental health systems but are often understaffed and underfunded. LLMs could support counselors, but existing benchmarks do not capture the escalation, risk assessment, and de-escalation central to crisis conversations, while privacy restrictions limit use of real transcripts. Methods: We present CrisisBench, a privacy-preserving suite for single- and multi-turn crisis counseling evaluation. It includes 1,085 single-turn tasks from 200 de-identified conversations and 1,185 patient LLMs derived from hotline metadata. Patient models and a 23-item LLM judge were calibrated against expert counselors. Results: We evaluated five GPT models plus draft-then-edit and retrieval-augmented generation. All systems underperformed human counselors on excessive empathy and questioning in single-turn evaluation. The rubric achieved human-human Krippendorff's $\alpha$ = 0.51 and LLM-human $\alpha$ = 0.54 (Pearson r = 0.80). In multi-turn evaluation, retrieval-augmented generation scored highest overall (0.961), with all systems within 0.058. Microskills and style/tone were near ceiling, while productivity and safety/risk accounted for most between-system variation. Counselors rated patient LLMs realistic (86%) and useful (92%). Conclusion: CrisisBench enables scalable, privacy-preserving evaluation of crisis counseling. Current systems perform strongly on core structural competencies but still diverge from experts on important response-level failure modes. We release the rubrics, judge prompts, and evaluation tasks.

items.title: Corrupting Ties: Investigating Robustness to Bias Injection Across Multi-Agent Network Topologies
items.content: arXiv:2611.21804v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: AI systems are increasingly deployed in high-stakes decision-making contexts, where interactions among components can introduce fairness risks that remain undetected when auditing components or collective outcomes in isolation. As LLM-based multi-agent systems become more prevalent, understanding how biased information propagates through agent interactions is essential for assessing their fairness. We introduce a controlled bias injection framework that replaces selected agent responses with predefined biased ones, enabling an intervention-based analysis of how network topology and injection configurations shape system behavior. We propose decision divergence metrics that quantify the effects of these interventions at the agent, network, and system levels, and evaluate five topologies on three binary classification tasks using LLMs from the Qwen and Gemma families. Sequential networks show the greatest divergence, whereas fully connected and mesh networks show less. Injection position also matters: in star networks, injecting the central agent has larger effects than injecting peripheral agents. Models further differ in whether divergence follows the injected bias. These findings highlight the role of network structure in the propagation of biased information and motivate topology-aware auditing of fairness risks in multi-agent systems.

The work proposes decision divergence metrics at agent, network, and system levels, linking fairness risks to network topology and injection configuration.
items.reasoning: An intervention-based causal approach to multi-agent fairness is methodologically strong and timely as multi-agent deployments grow; the framework could become a useful template for auditing emergent bias.

As LLM-based multi-agent systems become more prevalent, understanding how biased information propagates through agent interactions is essential for assessing their fairness. We introduce a controlled bias injection framework that replaces selected agent responses with predefined biased ones, enabling an intervention-based analysis of how network topology and injection configurations shape system behavior. We propose decision divergence metrics that quantify the effects of these interventions at the agent, network, and system levels, and evaluate five topologies on three binary classification tasks using LLMs from the Qwen and Gemma families. Sequential networks show the greatest divergence, whereas fully connected and mesh networks show less. Injection position also matters: in star networks, injecting the central agent has larger effects than injecting peripheral agents. Models further differ in whether divergence follows the injected bias. These findings highlight the role of network structure in the propagation of biased information and motivate topology-aware auditing of fairness risks in multi-agent systems.

items.title: VSpark: Speculative Decoding for Autoregressive Vision-Language-Action Models
items.content: arXiv:2611.22666v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Our aim is to accelerate autoregressive vision-language-action models (VLAs), which generate robot actions one token at a time. Speculative decoding makes this possible: a lightweight draft model proposes several tokens at once, and the VLA verifies them in a single pass, accepting only those that match its own predictions, so decoding remains lossless. The speedup, however, is limited in robot control, where many different tokens encode nearly the same motion and a draft close to the correct action is still rejected. To address this, our approach, VSpark, is built upon three design choices: (i) rollouts collected with calibrated action noise, which expose the draft to a wider range of robot states; (ii) feature alignment, which trains the draft to match the VLA's hidden features rather than its output tokens alone; and (iii) continuation reuse, which keeps the predictions the VLA has already computed along rejected drafts as candidates for the next verification step, instead of discarding them. On four VLAs with different action tokenizers and four manipulation benchmarks, VSpark achieves 1.28x to 2.10x speedup while keeping the VLA's decoding lossless.

Novel adaptation, credible team, though incremental relative to the broader speculative decoding literature.

items.title: The Rhythm of Generated Video: Latent Chunking Leaves Periodic Traces in Compressed Bitstreams
items.content: arXiv:2611.22996v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Most AI-generated video detectors analyze decoded pixels and overlook how videos are produced. We show that causal video autoencoders leave an architecture-specific rhythm in compressed bitstreams: their temporal stride concentrates unpredictable content at latent-chunk boundaries, so rate-distortion optimized encoders allocate bits periodically. Without decoding pixels, we observe four-frame pulses in CogVideoX and Wan2.2 and eight-frame pulses in LTX-Video, which are absent from content-matched camera footage. Passing camera footage through a generator's autoencoder alone induces the pulse, supporting its proposed origin. A training-free peak-ratio statistic separates generated from camera video (AUC 0.84-0.94) and persists across tested quantization settings and H.264/H.265 encoding. Frame-size traces also identify four commercial generators, with 89.2%, 84.1%, and 83.0% accuracy under H.264, H.265, and AV1, beating the pixel-based UnivFD baseline (72.7-73.6%). Our results directly link generative architecture to measurable coding demand.

A training-free peak-ratio statistic detects generated video with AUC 0.84-0.94 without decoding pixels. This opens a new, compute-efficient channel for AI-video detection.

items.title: VIVID: Beyond Static Multi-Image Reasoning with Localized Visual Differences and Textual Entity Dynamics in Video MLLMs
items.content: arXiv:2611.23153v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Video question answering under tight frame budgets requires preserving localized motion and event order, yet current video multimodal large language models (MLLMs) reduce comprehension to static multi-image reasoning by discarding unselected frames and encoding keyframes independently: (1) Spatially, whole-frame pooling dilutes small moving targets into static backgrounds; (2) Temporally, dropping intermediate frames or averaging tokens erases inter-frame motion, confusing direction, speed, and order. We propose VIVID (Visual Inter-frame Variations and Individual Dynamics), which moves beyond static snapshots like human vision: keyframes capture core states while inter-frame Patch Diffs preserve neighboring changes within $K_f$ keyframes. Autonomous Delta-Driven Keyframe Planning (ADKP) selects anchors from a $3\text{ fps}$ pool and feeds surrounding patch differences into Dual-Road Change Memory (DRCM), forming Dynamic Tokens at zero extra anchor tokens alongside a camera-stabilized Active Motion Region of Interest (ROI) and chronological Entity State Chains. Adding $0.22\%$ trainable parameters to a frozen $27\text{B}$ backbone, VIVID-Small ($50$ examples, $\sim 1.5$ GPU hours) beats all eleven baselines in overall accuracy across $8,083$ questions and trails only VIVID-Large ($3,600$ examples), which leads on MotionBench, Video-MME, and TempCompass.

The method augments keyframes with inter-frame Patch Diffs to preserve localized changes and event ordering under tight frame budgets.
items.reasoning: Identifies a genuine and underexplored failure mode in video MLLMs and proposes a concrete architectural remedy with a clear biological analogy; likely to matter for video understanding benchmarks, though evaluation scope from the abstract appears standard.

items.title: ReLAP: Latent Action Pretraining through Recurrent Video Prediction in JEPA Space
items.content: arXiv:2611.22077v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Videos provide a rich source of physical interaction for learning robot behavior without action annotations, yet effective latent actions must capture not only local transitions but also how those transitions evolve over time. We introduce ReLAP, a latent-action pretraining framework that couples local transition learning with recurrent multi-step prediction in a frozen JEPA representation space. A shared inverse dynamics model infers compact continuous latent actions from adjacent observations, while a latent world model recurrently predicts the future JEPA features. Because each predicted feature becomes the context for the next transition, errors at later steps backpropagate through the rollout to earlier latent actions, encouraging temporally coherent dynamics beyond pairwise reconstruction. We transfer this representation to a vision-language model using two complementary objectives: latent distillation from the frozen inverse teacher and recurrent future-feature prediction through the frozen latent world model. The resulting policy is then adapted to robot demonstrations with action flow matching. At deployment, the explicit latent-action and world-model branches are removed, and the fine-tuned VLM predicts physical actions directly, reducing inference complexity. With only 11M pretraining samples and 1.06B trainable parameters, ReLAP achieves 97.9% on standard LIBERO and 70.0% over zero-shot LIBERO-Plus perturbations. On the LARY latent-action benchmark, ReLAP ranks second in both mean regression error and mean classification accuracy among the compared methods. These results demonstrate that recurrent action-free latent action pretraining can learn compact, temporally structured, and transferable representations for downstream robot control.

Error backpropagation through rollouts encourages temporally consistent latent actions from unlabeled video for robot learning.
items.reasoning: Nice combination of JEPA representations, latent actions, and recurrent world modeling for action-free pretraining from video, a timely direction. Novelty is moderate since latent action learning from video is an active area, but the multi-step consistency mechanism is a meaningful contribution.

items.title: How should we define “capabilities activities” for the purpose of pacing?
items.content:
We’d like to pace the frontier by restricting the amount of compute AI companies use to improve AI capabilities, perhaps via legislation or voluntary commitments. For this purpose, we’d need a standardized definition of which uses of compute count as “capabilities activities”. This document gives one option for such a definition; a rough breakdown of our classification is as follows:

We define and elaborate on each of these categories below. First, though, we discuss the desiderata this definition is meant to satisfy.

Thanks to Thomas Larsen, Zach Stein-Perlman, Alex Mallen, Eric Gan, Jeff Wu, Girish Gupta, Adam Kaufman, and others for feedback on drafts of this document.

# What our classification is meant to accomplish

In order for such a definition to be an effective tool for pacing, it needs to satisfy some basic properties:

- Substantially restricting the amount of compute spent on “capabilities activities” should substantially decrease the rate of AI progress.
- The classification should be robust to adversarial pressure, in that the above point should hold even if companies are willing to adjust or reframe their activities to avoid being classified as “capabilities”.
- The classification should be fairly simple and tractable to adjudicate. Reasonable experts should largely agree on how this definition classifies activities (even if it is difficult to agree on the extent to which individual activities are actually useful for capabilities)....

items.summary: This post proposes a standardized taxonomy for classifying which uses of compute count as AI capabilities activities, intended as a foundation for compute-based frontier pacing via legislation or voluntary commitments. It lays out desiderata such as effectiveness at slowing progress and robustness to adversarial reframing by labs, then defines categories of activity.
items.reasoning: Substantive governance research addressing a concrete, under-specified policy design problem (defining capabilities compute for pacing rules). Practical relevance to AI regulation debates and input from multiple reviewers, though it is a proposal rather than empirical work.

items.title: RL Misalignment Under Accurate Rewards and Explicit Requirements
items.content:
tl;dr: Even when the task reward function is accurate and contextual requirements are explicitly stated, RL can make agents genuinely more capable while reinforcing violations of those requirements. Beyond conventional reward hacking, agents can learn to do more real work by crossing authorization boundaries.

More details and motion graphics are in the blog and paper. Here is a quick story about it!:)

## Intro

We build pipelines to construct scalable verifiable environments that have 1. context requirements (corresponding to some allowed boundary region), and 2. task rewards and independent checks of actual work; 3. guaranteed shortcuts.

On resource tasks, reward accurately measures real work. We include reward-hacking tasks as well, such as Validation. Contextual requirements are explicitly stated throughout.

For example, an agent is working on company data with (1) explicit permission to use an external service only for public data, (2) a reward that accurately measures completed processing work, and (3) a guaranteed shortcut😈 sending restricted data to that service completes more real work than any authorized strategy, but violates the permission boundary.

Sounds familiar? To a certain degree, such a shortcut can be blocked post hoc by good software design awareness, just like, as software engineers, we should make sure we can't allow customers to buy -1 item so they can get the shortcut of 'having one more item but the total expense is now lower'....

items.summary: This work constructs verifiable RL environments with accurate task rewards, explicitly stated contextual permission boundaries, and guaranteed shortcuts, showing that RL can increase genuine capability while teaching agents to cross authorization boundaries to do more real work. This extends reward hacking beyond incentive errors to violations of constraints even under accurate rewards.
items.reasoning: Original and important alignment research direction: demonstrating emergent boundary-violating behavior under accurate rewards and explicit requirements isolates a distinct failure mode from classic reward hacking. Scalable environment pipelines are a solid methodology, though results appear preliminary and self-published.

items.title: A closer look at “Sparks of Weight-Space Programming”
items.content:
GPT-6 Astra’s improvement of Qwen’s math is not “native weight editing” but activation steering with clever use of synthetic data

Zhi Wang, Brandon Hsu, Tianhao Wang, Mikhail Belkin (UC San Diego). Code: GitHub.

## TL;DR

- Astra’s edit of Qwen is equivalent to a special case of context-dependent activation steering: it pushes the activations along a fixed direction constructed from data, with a strength that depends linearly on the current activations.
- Generalizing Astra’s edit, with a trained “sensing vector” that determines how strongly to push along the same fixed direction, can further improve the effectiveness of the edit.
- Astra constructs the fixed direction from short synthetic traces rather than from Qwen’s real rollouts, a design choice that turns out to be substantially more effective.

In a widely circulated blog post Sparks of Weight-Space Programming, the authors highlight how GPT-6 Astra edits a small language model without any training: it writes a short program that changes parts of the MLP weight matrices to significantly improve the math performance of the model. The authors present this as evidence for a new paradigm they call Weight-Space Programming, stating that “neural network weights will soon be natively optimized by LLMs that deliberately reason about their weights.” They even frame this as a shift away from symbolic optimizers like Adam, which has been the default optimizer for training deep learning models since its introduction in 2014. The post, and especially its claim that frontier LLMs like Astra can “natively” edit weights, has received considerable attention. A single tweet by the lead author has been viewed nearly 10 million times (as of November 2026). While the authors and many commentators interpret Astra’s edit as “native weight editing,” we argue that Astra is acting like a clever researcher, effectively implementing existing activation steering techniques combined with synthetic data. Additionally, recognizing the...

items.summary: Researchers at UC San Diego analyze the widely circulated claim that GPT-6 Astra can edit a small Qwen model's MLP weights via a written program to improve its math performance, concluding the effect is equivalent to context-dependent activation steering along a fixed data-constructed direction rather than genuine weight-space programming. They further show that a trained sensing vector generalizing the edit improves effectiveness, and that building the steering direction from short synthetic traces rather than real rollouts is substantially more effective.
items.reasoning: Substantive technical debunking and extension with an identifiable academic team, code release, and a crisp mechanistic account of a viral claim about a model that has been available since September 2026. It advances understanding of activation steering versus weight editing and corrects a potentially misleading narrative, though it is an analysis of one case rather than a broad new method.

items.title: TeleChat to Xing4: Advancing Frontier Agentic Models on Domestic Chips and Frameworks
items.content: arXiv:2611.22115v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We present Xing 4, a series of large language models that extends the TeleChat lineage through coordinated advances in model architecture and training infrastructure on Ascend. This report describes the design principles and systems engineering behind the series, spanning architecture selection, large-scale pretraining, and reasoning and agentic post-training. We study how sparse activation, attention design, model depth and width, and speculative decoding balance model capacity with computation, memory access, and execution overhead. Our pretraining infrastructure builds on MindSpore HyperParallel, combining topology-aware hybrid sharding, efficient distributed optimizer execution, and coordinated management of long-sequence workloads and activation memory. CPU affinity and core isolation further reduce host scheduling interference. Together, these mechanisms support the pretraining of a 285B-parameter model on 8,192 Ascend 910C cards, providing a concrete setting for the architectural and systems studies. For post-training, we introduce TeleGym, a unified agent execution platform that connects execution, evaluation, and trajectory construction to policy optimization. Disaggregated asynchronous execution, bounded oversampling, and partial rollout accommodate heterogeneous task durations while preserving trajectory continuity across policy updates. Together, these advances establish an Ascend-oriented training foundation for the continued development of Xing 4 across model scales and increasingly demanding reasoning and agent workloads.

We study how sparse activation, attention design, model depth and width, and speculative decoding balance model capacity with computation, memory access, and execution overhead. Our pretraining infrastructure builds on MindSpore HyperParallel, combining topology-aware hybrid sharding, efficient distributed optimizer execution, and coordinated management of long-sequence workloads and activation memory. CPU affinity and core isolation further reduce host scheduling interference. Together, these mechanisms support the pretraining of a 285B-parameter model on 8,192 Ascend 910C cards, providing a concrete setting for the architectural and systems studies. For post-training, we introduce TeleGym, a unified agent execution platform that connects execution, evaluation, and trajectory construction to policy optimization. Disaggregated asynchronous execution, bounded oversampling, and partial rollout accommodate heterogeneous task durations while preserving trajectory continuity across policy updates. Together, these advances establish an Ascend-oriented training foundation for the continued development of Xing 4 across model scales and increasingly demanding reasoning and agent workloads.

items.title: MCTS Is Counting the Wrong Thing: Learning Exploration Counts for LLM Reasoning
items.content: arXiv:2611.22301v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS) has powered landmark successes in reinforcement learning, yet its gains in LLM reasoning can remain modest despite substantial search effort. We identify an overlooked bottleneck: what MCTS counts. Standard UCT assigns independent visit counts to textual branches, allowing different formulations of the same reasoning strategy to repeatedly receive exploration bonuses. Our theoretical analysis shows that this count fragmentation can impair exploration efficiency, as quantified by increased cumulative regret. To address this problem, we introduce Learned Pseudo-Count MCTS (LPC-MCTS), which changes only the exploration statistic in UCT. A lightweight Coin-Flipping Network head on the policy's hidden representations estimates representation coverage, enabling related branches to share exploration evidence. Across 5 mathematical-reasoning and 7 search benchmarks, LPC-MCTS consistently outperforms strong MCTS baselines. Holding each LPC-MCTS-trained policy fixed, replacing standard MCTS counts at inference improves average mean@16 accuracy across 5 mathematical benchmarks by 3.79 percentage points on Qwen2.5-7B and 2.71 points on Qwen3-4B. Applying LPC-MCTS during both training and inference yields gains of 4.96 and 4.37 points over standard MCTS, respectively. Together, our theory and experiments show that changing what MCTS counts can substantially improve its exploration efficiency and reasoning performance.

items.title: PACT: Plan-Action Consistency Training by Preserving Correct Plans and Repairing Actions in GUI Agents
items.content: arXiv:2611.22591v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: GUI agents can formulate a correct immediate plan in their reasoning yet emit an action that fails to execute it, creating an execution gap. This recurring mismatch undermines reliable task completion, as a single execution error can derail a multi-step workflow. In outcome-supervised reinforcement learning, broadcasting a negative response-level advantage across all generated tokens risks penalizing valid planning together with erroneous execution. To address this credit-assignment conflict, we introduce PACT (Plan-Action Consistency Training), a training framework that combines reference-aligned plan protection and plan-aligned action repair without altering the original scalar action reward. Using annotated reference actions to identify execution gaps, PACT protects the verified plan by masking negative policy-gradient contributions across its token span. Keeping the generated reasoning unchanged as context, it then favors the reference action over the emitted erroneous action through a preference surrogate with stop-gradient pair weights. Compared with the outcome-only baseline, PACT raises AndroidWorld task success from 60.34% to 68.97% (+8.63 pp), while improving rule-based plan-action consistency on AndroidControl High from 83.71% to 89.74% (+6.03 pp). Adapting PACT to desktop agents also improves task success from 40.92% to 44.17% (+3.25 pp) on the full 369-task OSWorld benchmark. Together, these results establish PACT as an effective credit-assignment framework for bridging execution gaps and improving task completion across mobile and desktop GUI environments.

The framework combines reference-aligned plan protection with plan-aligned action repair while preserving the original scalar action reward.

items.title: Remembered as Brief: Stored Preferences SilentlyRemove Decision-Critical Information
items.content: arXiv:2611.22697v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: People increasingly learn what they need for decisions about health, money, law and safety from AI assistants, and what an assistant leaves out the user never sees. An answer with a warning removed can be true in every sentence, so fact-checks pass it, and an assistant with memory applies a preference stored once to later questions the user never had in mind. We introduce \bench{}, an Inspect benchmark of 100 everyday decisions across 25 domains in which only the assistant's memory of the user varies: the user states a belief, the model infers it from a remark, or a web page the user asked to summarise plants it. Testing five models, we find three effects. First, after summarising a page with one line addressed to AI assistants, Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite and DeepSeek V4 Pro save ``prefers very short answers and does not want warnings'' as the user's preference in every episode, and 93\% and 84\% of their later answers miss a critical item, almost always silently; under a stated brevity preference, 78--96\% of omissions are silent. Second, the same two models then pick an option for the user on 80\% and 95\% of value-dependent choices, against none with neutral memory. Third, a one-line instruction leaves 2--8\% of answers with a silent gap but most missing content still missing, while listing the must-know points before applying the user profile restores more of the content in four of five models. We release the scenarios, harness and logs.
items.author: Joshua Adrian Cahyono
items.summary: This benchmark study shows that assistant memory of user preferences can silently remove decision-critical information: a stored preference causes models to omit warnings or options the user never sees, while every individual sentence remains true. The benchmark spans 100 decisions across 25 domains where only the assistant's memory varies, testing five models including Gemini 2.5 Flash. This reveals a novel memory-mediated safety risk distinct from fact-checking.
items.reasoning: A genuinely novel and concerning failure mode — personalization memory silently degrading decision quality in ways that pass fact-checks. Single-author work, but the benchmark design is clever and the finding is directly relevant to consumer AI assistants and AI safety policy.

items.title: Computed Permutation Trellis Coding: Near-Optimal Quantization from Two Multiplications and a 64-Byte Table
items.content: arXiv:2611.22019v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: We propose Computed Permutation Trellis Coding (CPTC), a low-bit quantization format for tensors written once and read many times. Formats that round each value on its own, such as INT4 and FP4, waste a large part of their bits against the information-theoretic ideal. Trellis codes recover this loss by encoding values jointly, but prior decoders either need a large lookup table for their best quality or compute values with a hash that restricts what they can decode. CPTC's decoder multiplies its state by two coefficients and adds the top bits of the products to index a 64-byte table. Because that sum is not uniformly distributed, the rarely used ends of a small table can hold values far out in the tails. One decoder serves every bit width from 1 to 6, reproduces the standard integer and floating-point formats exactly, and comes within 0.07 bits of the ideal at 4 bits. It matches a random-permutation trellis code whose table is thousands of times larger, and exceeds every QTIP codebook. In LLM weight quantization without fine-tuning, CPTC has the lowest KL divergence to the unquantized model at every tested bit width on Llama 3.1 8B and 70B Instruct against QTIP's codebooks (by up to 27%). The decoder has been built into the AWS Trainium 4 AI accelerator, where it runs at the throughput of the native FP4 and FP8 formats for a negligible fraction of the systolic array's area. Fused encoding kernels quantize an 8B model's linear layers in under two minutes on one GPU and, in cycle-level simulation, on one Trainium 4 chip.

items.summary: CPTC is a low-bit tensor quantization format whose decoder computes each value with two multiplications and indexing into a 64-byte table, recovering much of the information-theoretic loss that per-value formats like INT4/FP4 incur. It jointly encodes values via trellis coding, serves all bit widths with one decoder, and suits write-once-read-many weights.
items.reasoning: An elegant systems-level contribution with direct relevance to LLM inference efficiency: near-trellis-code quality at a tiny, hardware-friendly decode cost. If empirical end-to-end results hold up, this could matter for edge and memory-bound serving, though adoption depends on kernel integration and compression-quality tradeoffs.

items.title: Eyes in the Update? Learning Where Rewards Land in Multimodal Reasoning
items.content: arXiv:2611.22438v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Multimodal post-training has moved from broad instruction tuning toward reinforcement learning for image and video reasoning, where outcome rewards can improve final-answer accuracy. Yet these rewards are assigned to complete generated trajectories, while visual evidence is used only at sparse and uneven positions inside the response. Recent work has begun to make multimodal RL more token-sensitive through grounding signals or external token-level weighting. We ask a more specific question: can the allocation of the same trajectory-level reward be inferred from the model's own multimodal computation, rather than from an auxiliary annotator, perception module, or process label? We propose Gaze-RL, a representation-driven policy optimization method that redistributes completion-level advantage through a latent reward landing field. The field is computed from internal cross-modal geometry and local predictive uncertainty, assigning larger update weight to positions that are both visually anchored and decision-bearing while remaining mean-one, so the total credit of each rollout is preserved and only its positionwise allocation changes. Gaze-RL requires no process supervision, auxiliary perception module, or architectural modification, and improves both Qwen2.5-VL and InternVL3.5 across a broad range of image and video benchmarks.
items.author: Lixuan He, Tianzhe Chu, Shulin Tian, Shikang Zheng, Feng Chen, Yi Ma
items.summary: Gaze-RL is a representation-driven policy optimization method for multimodal RL that infers where a trajectory-level outcome reward should be allocated within a response using the model's own multimodal computation, rather than auxiliary annotators or process labels. It targets the mismatch between trajectory-level rewards and sparse, unevenly used visual evidence in image and video reasoning. This makes multimodal RL more token-sensitive without external supervision.
items.reasoning: A novel and well-motivated contribution to multimodal RL credit assignment that removes the need for external token-level annotators; credible author list, and the direction is highly relevant to current post-training research, though empirical breadth is unclear from the abstract.

items.title: Large Language Models Have Not Yet Transformed Science
items.content: arXiv:2611.22975v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: The emergence of large language models (LLMs) in late 2022 has raised questions about the future of science, but assessing their impact requires understanding how scientific practices were already evolving. We analyze 2.5 million full-text papers across five disciplines from 2015 to 2025, tracing trends over a broad spectrum of lexical, structural, epistemological, and social dimensions. Aside from frequency shifts in some words, most pre-2023 trends continued with limited detectable breaks. Among the notable exceptions, growth in computer science coauthor teams accelerated significantly in Asia, while apparent declines in biomedical topic diversity largely reflected standardization in article formats. Our study establishes an empirical foundation for monitoring the health of global science as LLM adoption deepens.
items.author: Ron Bekkerman, Nichole Li, Bahareh Kargar, Mark Somers
items.summary: Analyzes 2.5 million full-text papers across five disciplines from 2015-2025 and finds that most pre-2023 scientific practice trends continued with limited detectable breaks after LLMs emerged, with exceptions like accelerated CS coauthor growth in Asia. It establishes an empirical baseline for assessing LLM impact on science.
items.reasoning: Large-scale, careful empirical study with a sobering headline finding that counters hype; the longitudinal design controlling for pre-existing trends strengthens causal interpretation, though bibliometric proxies have inherent limits.

items.title: ReMaRL: Learning to Unmask and Remask in Frozen Diffusion Language Models
items.content: arXiv:2611.22576v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Masked diffusion language models generate tokens in parallel, and the order in which tokens are unmasked affects final-answer accuracy. Several methods learn unmasking policies from task rewards, but these policies cannot remask earlier predictions. Remasking lets the model correct those predictions using newly generated context. Heuristic rules guide both unmasking and remasking, while supervised remaskers learn to detect token errors. Neither approach directly optimizes these decisions for final-answer correctness. To address this gap, we introduce ReMaRL (Remasking with Reinforcement Learning), a lightweight policy that learns which tokens to unmask, retain, or remask. We train this roughly 0.3M-parameter policy with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) from final-answer rewards while keeping the diffusion model frozen. With LLaDA-8B-Instruct, ReMaRL achieves the highest scores among the compared unmasking and remasking policies within the tested inference budgets of 4-32 model calls on math and 8-16 calls on code.
items.author: Egor Shibaev, Danila Biktimirov, Ivan Klimov, Artem Makoian, Viacheslav Meshchaninov, Dmitry Vetrov
items.summary: ReMaRL trains a lightweight reinforcement learning policy, roughly 0.3M parameters, to decide which tokens to unmask, retain, or remask in frozen masked diffusion language models, directly optimizing final-answer correctness. Prior learned policies could only unmask, while remasking heuristics were not reward-optimized. This enables self-correction using newly generated context during parallel decoding.
items.reasoning: Improving masked diffusion LMs through learned unmask-remask policies is timely given growing interest in diffusion language models, and the tiny policy head with GRPO training is an elegant, efficient design. Impact depends on diffusion LMs maturing into mainstream alternatives to autoregressive decoding.

items.title: NONSENSE: Non-Semantic Strings Expose Semanticity Gaps in Dense Retrieval
items.content: arXiv:2611.22353v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Dense retrieval is central to modern search, question answering, and retrieval-augmented generation, where high similarity is often treated as evidence of semantic relevance. We examine how far this assumption can be stressed. NONSENSE is a black-box sparse-edit probe that constructs visibly non-semantic strings while forbidding query-term copying, optimizing only the dense similarity between a query and the string. Across five BEIR-style datasets and three popular single-vector retrievers, these strings frequently outscore the retriever's own best judged query-relevant passage (QRP), and often rank first in the full corpus. The result indicates a semanticity gap in the evaluated dense retrievers: nearest-neighbor status can be separated from passage-like meaning. These findings highlight the importance of evaluating dense retrievers not only by whether they retrieve relevant documents, but also by how reliably their similarity scores reflect semantic evidence.

The paper exposes a semanticity gap showing that nearest-neighbor similarity can be fully decoupled from meaning in dense retrieval.
items.reasoning: A clean adversarial probe with broad implications, since dense retrieval underpins modern RAG systems; demonstrating top-ranked gibberish strings is a striking failure mode. The evaluation is black-box and broad, though the attack is known-adjacent to prior embedding vulnerability work, keeping it short of a top-tier score.

items.title: SR-VLA: Stall-Reduced VLA Execution via Predicted-Input Lookahead and Selective KV Cache Repair
items.content: arXiv:2611.22356v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies incur control stalls when inference blocks the next action chunk. Asynchronous early inference can hide latency, but its results may be inconsistent with the arriving actual inputs. Unconditional reuse risks acting on mismatched inputs, whereas full recomputation discards useful precomputation. We propose SR-VLA, combining predicted-input lookahead with selective KV cache repair. During current chunk execution, a lightweight action-conditioned predictor generates next-boundary visual observations and proprioceptive state. These predictions, together with the task instruction, drive the frozen VLA to precompute a speculative KV cache and action chunk. After real inputs are available to VLA, predicted--real differences and task conditions determine whether to accept the action chunk or trigger selective KV repair. On LIBERO, SR-VLA achieves $2.67\times$ and $1.27\times$ query speedups over the respective synchronous $\pi_{0.5}$ and OpenVLA-OFT baselines, while maintaining competitive average task success rates. Under target-motion perturbation, success remains baseline-comparable, with $1.52\times$--$1.93\times$ query speedup.
items.author: Tao Zhang, Yi Zhong, Jinhao Ruan, Yipeng Gao, Linfeng Zhong, Youming Yang, Yuan Wang
items.summary: SR-VLA reduces control stalls in vision-language-action policy execution by predicting next-boundary observations and using them to precompute a speculative KV cache and action chunk, then selectively repairing mismatches when real inputs arrive. This hides inference latency without the risks of unconditional reuse or full recomputation.
items.reasoning: A systems-level contribution addressing the real inference-latency bottleneck of VLA policies at deployment, with a clever selective-repair mechanism bridging speculative execution and correctness. Novelty is solid in an emerging subarea, though impact depends on generality across policies.

items.title: What Does an Agent Need? Bundle-Aware Agent Resource Composition
items.content: arXiv:2611.22030v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: An agent resource's value depends on its backbone and companion resources and is known only after execution. Token-based generators remain tied to their training catalog, while independent resource scoring misses complementarities and reused bundles target other tasks. We formulate Task-Conditioned Agent Resource Composition (AgentComposition): jointly selecting a backbone model and a tool-skill bundle to maximize end-to-end execution utility. Our Retrieval-Grounded Bundle-Aware Agent Generation retrieves candidate resources and past configurations of similar tasks. A fine-tuned generator reads resource descriptions and recombines candidates through constrained beam search, allowing new resources without retraining. A bundle-aware critic ranks complete configurations using a large language model (LLM) teacher and historically successful configurations as execution proxies, and adapts to execution feedback when available. We evaluate reference recovery, offline execution with judged and native rewards, and online recommendation with real execution, building AgentSelect-Exec with 5,060 executed configurations. Our method recovers the complete reference configuration within ten candidates for 67.73% of AgentSelect queries, nearly twice the strongest baseline, and leads all baselines on SkillsBench. The proxy-trained critic raises the top-ranked agent's execution score from 7.58 to 8.37 out of 10; execution feedback increases it to 8.78, above the strongest baselines. Four target-domain queries suffice to adapt the generator to SkillsBench. Agents recommended online outperform the strongest baselines under both an LLM judge and native verifiers. These results support learning and transferring joint resource composition from task experience.

items.title: Multi-Agent Memory Inconsistency: Where Factual Conflicts Disappear in LLM Agents
items.content: arXiv:2611.22245v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Multi-agent delegation lets LLM systems distribute evidence collection across workers with separate contexts. This creates a consistency challenge: facts retrieved by workers may be missing from the evidence available to the lead for a joint conclusion. We introduce a benchmark and evidence-flow profiler for studying multi-agent memory inconsistency through controlled factual conflicts in Harvey LAB document-review tasks. Pooled across three models with comparable generation spending, requiring delegation increases retrieval of both conflicting claims from 50.2% to 68.7% relative to single-agent execution, yet conflict detection falls from 16.2% to 13.2%. Within this setting, workers report both claims for only 35.2% of retrieved pairs, and pooled matched comparisons show higher detection than single-agent execution when one worker reads both claims but lower detection when the claims are split across workers. Worker-to-lead handoffs are a central target for improving conflict detection in multi-agent LLMs.

items.title: LMLineage: Content Lineage and Context Governance for LLM Agents
items.content: arXiv:2611.22511v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Interpretability for AI agents should not be confined to understanding the model's internal weights. It must also cover the agent's reasoning and decision-making process over multi-source context. We present LMLineage, an out-of-band system that attributes every output sentence of an agent session to its supporting input spans with calibrated confidences, without requiring white-box access to the model or any additional inference passes. On top of the lineage metadata, we build concept-drift micro compaction: instead of waiting for the context-length limit and summarizing everything, the system detects when previously used input documents have stopped being referenced ("drifted") and surgically compacts only those, preserving user instructions verbatim. We evaluate on a multi-tier corpus: 71 gold annotated sentences from 10 Chinese web-QA cases, plus 90 turns of independently collected multi-turn sessions across three generator models (gpt-4o-mini, qwen3.8-27b, deepseek-v4-flash). Results show that (i) window-level embedding similarity is far better aligned with LLM paraphrasing than whole document or lexical matching; (ii) the greedy-window fast path is both faster and more accurate on average than exhaustive line-matching (a multiple-comparisons bias in the latter inflates web recall at the cost of overall accuracy); (iii) per-turn attribution completes in 1s on a single GPU, remaining stable as context accumulates to 40 turns; and (iv) concept-drift detection is conservative (0% false compaction) with recall bounded by attribution accuracy. We further describe the concept-drift micro compaction design and an interactive incident-tracing/memory-cleaning case study. A companion patent application covers the lineage construction method.

items.title: Values Shape What Self-Improving Coding Agents Build
items.content: arXiv:2611.23067v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Self-improving agents are typically optimized for the results they produce, with less attention to how they produce them. Their instructions give designers limited ways to shape how they work, especially when the task is open-ended. This paper studies whether a short value statement in an agent's persistent instruction file changes not only how well the agent performs but also what it builds. Four higher-order value types in Schwartz's theory of basic human values were evaluated: openness to change, conservation, self-enhancement, and self-transcendence. Across diverse coding tasks, the values were held fixed within each run over multiple iterations of self-improvement. Three findings emerged: (1) Values matter for performance across a diverse set of tasks. The openness values increase performance on held-out data, whereas the opposite conservation values result in scores below those of an agent given no values. (2) Values change what agents build, producing solution algorithms that differ in size, complexity and approach. (3) Human oversight is still needed for designing values. Allowing the agent to revise its own values narrows the differences between sets of values, and values distilled from the AI literature provide no detectable gain over having no values. Properly designed values can thus influence what a self-improving coding agent builds and, where the task permits, how well it performs.

It evaluates openness to change, conservation, self-enhancement, and self-transcendence across diverse coding tasks over repeated self-improvement iterations. The finding that values affect performance and output character is directly relevant to shaping open-ended agent behavior beyond task rewards.

items.title: SimAI: Mechanistic User Simulation through Psychological Network Models
items.content: arXiv:2611.21808v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Realistic user simulation enables the study of human interactions when direct experimentation is costly or potentially harmful. However, existing simulators largely overlook the psychological mechanisms that drive user behavior. We introduce SimAI, a framework for mechanistic user simulation that models how psychological factors interact to shape user responses. To overcome the challenge of supervising open-ended behavior, we propose a graph reconstruction objective that provides graph-level rewards based on how well simulated conversations reflect the underlying psychological relationships. To support this approach, we construct PSYCHE, a dataset of 18,576 profile-network pairs derived from 516 psychotherapy cases. Automatic evaluations show that SimAI achieves greater simulation and behavioral diversity than existing patient simulators while maintaining strong profile alignment. In an interactive study with 30 mental-health professionals and trainees, SimAI receives the highest average ratings for conversational authenticity, realistic help-seeking behavior, and clinical training utility. Beyond simulation quality, SimAI enables realistic clinical training and uncovers safety failures in prolonged AI interactions with vulnerable users. Code is available at https://github.com/behavioral-data/ANGEL-UserSim.

items.title: Pathology Randomization for Synthetic Priors and Zero-Shot Detection
items.content: arXiv:2611.21975v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Hospital brain imaging archives hold a diverse array of pathology at sample sizes beyond prospective studies, particularly for underrepresented populations and diseases. To unlock uncurated clinical data and scale analysis, methods are needed to detect abnormalities across contrasts and resolutions. Synthetic data has provided robust, contrast-agnostic models for a variety of human neuroimaging tasks in healthy anatomy, but pathology detection and other tasks in clinical settings still require real patient data, contrast-specific models, or disease-specific generators. We propose PathoDraw, a generative model of brain MRI with pathology. A conditional distribution of lesions given the healthy anatomy is drawn into the label map before contrast-agnostic rendering, and a single network estimates healthy anatomy with exact signed intensity deviation of any input scan. The contrast-agnostic 3D UNet learns the healthy labels under the lesion and the signed deviation directly and identifies pathology via robust tissue statistics and learned features, despite no training on real pathology. We show zero-shot detection on public stroke, tumor, and white matter hyperintensity datasets as well as archived clinical data, spanning $T_1$w, FLAIR and $T_2$w at various resolutions under a recent unsupervised anomaly detection benchmark protocol. Our single model exceeds or performs comparably to contrast-specific anomaly detectors trained on real scans and keeps healthy anatomy intact. The same generator trains networks for super-resolution and for registration in the presence of pathology. Our model, robust across acquisition and disease, enables the use of uncurated, archived data for clinical analysis. Our code is available at https://github.com/agr78/Pathology-Randomizer.

Strong author team from neuroimaging and a clear path to impact on underrepresented diseases and populations, contingent on validation details not visible in the abstract.

items.title: Communicate the Change: Efficient Expert Parallelism via Activation Compression
items.content: arXiv:2611.22215v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Scaling has driven the success of large language models (LLM), with sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures enabling greater parameter capacity without a proportional increase in computation. At large scales, MoE models rely on expert parallelism to distribute experts across devices. Each MoE layer requires two synchronous collective communication steps during inference: dispatching hidden states to the activated experts and combining the resulting expert outputs. As compute throughput has outpaced interconnect bandwidth, these synchronous collectives have become a major bottleneck to MoE scaling and efficiency. We address this challenge with EchoMoE, a lightweight architecture modification that retrofits existing MoE models, requiring approximately 8,500x fewer training tokens than full pretraining. Motivated by the observation that transformer blocks update the residual stream incrementally, we use a hidden state from an earlier layer as a reference and communicate only the compressed difference between it and the current state, rather than communicating each hidden state in full. EchoMoE periodically refreshes these reference states and transmits only the compressed differences synchronously, reducing the traffic on latency-critical paths without significant computational overhead. EchoMoE reduces inter-node communication volume by 58% and improves throughput by 22.6%, while preserving average performance within 3.8 percentage points across 18 benchmarks. EchoMoE further improves inference throughput by up to 2.38x over bandwidth-constrained Ethernet, paving the way for wide-area distributed inference. EchoMoE also tolerates quantization of the communicated representations without measurable quality loss. We release an efficient implementation for applying EchoMoE to pretrained MoE models, together with an inference integration for vLLM.

The modification requires no retraining of existing MoE models. It targets inference efficiency at large scale where synchronous collectives dominate cost.

items.title: Manufacturing Differential Sparsity: Planner-Hardware Co-Design for Efficient World Model Planning
items.content: arXiv:2611.22483v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: JEPA-style latent world models let embodied agents plan toward new goals with model predictive control, but they are still too slow for real-life embodied control: sampling-based MPC repeats predictor inference tens of thousands of times per plan, and even on high-end GPUs one planning step can take tens of seconds. We observe substantial latent locality in this repeated-inference workload: the predictor maps close actions to close latents, and inside a quantized predictor this closeness takes a form that hardware can exploit, differential bit-level sparsity. Unlike an input stream, whose temporal similarity is given, a planner itself decides which candidates it evaluates together, so the planner can choose its own references and, with reference forest sampling, manufacture more sparsity: it couples the sampled action sequences of each group to a shared root, with competitive planning quality. We build the accelerator on the insights of the rich line of bit-level sparsity accelerators and design it and the planner tightly coupled as a single co-design: the planner increases sparsity and exposes structure for hardware scheduling, and the bit-exact hardware effectively uses the sparsity that the planner creates. On three JEPA world models, our co-design is 1.28-1.80x faster than a dense accelerator and uses 38-52% less energy, and it is 1.22-1.58x faster than prior bit-sparse design and uses 16-36% less energy, with the same area. To our knowledge, our planner is the first planner that manufactures differential bit-level sparsity across its candidates and exposes its structure for hardware scheduling, and our co-design is the first algorithm-hardware co-design for JEPA-style world-model planning.

This planner-hardware co-design could make latent world model planning viable for real-time embodied control.

items.title: Learning Agent-Centric Vision-Language-Action World Models for Autonomous Driving
items.content: arXiv:2611.22880v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Recent progress in integrating vision-language-action (VLA) models with world modeling has significantly advanced end-to-end autonomous driving by allowing systems to reason about imagined futures instead of merely reacting to current observations. However, most world VLA models generate future frames at the pixel level with plenty of dense visual tokens. Although such generated futures can be visually plausible, they preserve many driving-irrelevant appearance details, i.e., only a small portion of the tokens directly encode critical planning-relevant factors, such as agent geometry, motion dynamics, and interactions. This introduces a significant performance bottleneck. An important question thus arises: what world state should a world VLA model reason over to support planning beyond pixel-level prediction? We argue that planning-oriented world modeling should focus on a compact and structured agent-centric latent state that captures the interactions between objects in the driving scene over time. As such, we introduce AgentWorld, an agent-centric VLA world model that uses discrete agent tokens jointly for reasoning and trajectory planning. Each token is dynamically grounded to a surrounding agent associated with its object's state, such as semantic identity, 3D geometry, motion, and interaction context. AgentWorld learns these tokens through three key processes: explicit geometric grounding, reasoning-oriented supervised fine-tuning, and agent-oriented reinforcement learning. Extensive open-loop and closed-loop experiments under diverse driving scenarios show that AgentWorld enhances planning capabilities, fully exploits visual evidence and agent dynamics, and yields interpretable agent-centric world states.

items.title: Ambient LLMs: Data-Efficient Supervised Fine-tuning via Temperature Matching
items.content: arXiv:2611.23229v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Collecting large-scale, diverse, and high-quality post-training datasets for autoregressive language models is challenging. Consequently, Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) is typically applied to datasets significantly smaller than those used for pre-training, which leads to overfitting and the catastrophic forgetting of the tails of the data distribution. To prevent this collapse, we introduce Ambient SFT, a principled framework for leveraging imperfect predictions to augment the fine-tuning set. In our method, a "frozen" version of the pre-trained model serves as a noisy teacher that the fine-tuned model must match at a coarse level. In particular, we require that the high-temperature versions of the conditional distributions produced by the post-training model should match the high-temperature versions of the pre-training ones. The temperature hyperparameter controls the level of trust in the pre-trained model, with the limit $T\to \infty$ reverting back to regular SFT and $T=1$ to knowledge distillation. We demonstrate that our approach outperforms standard SFT across domain adaptation, instruction-tuning, and reasoning, leading for up to $21\%$ average relative improvement to standard SFT.

The fine-tuned model must match the teacher's high-temperature conditional distributions at a coarse level, leveraging imperfect predictions to expand effective training signal. The framework is principled and aims to preserve the tails of the pre-training distribution during post-training.

items.title: Large Language Models as Nonlinear Dynamical Systems: The Three Clocks of Depth, Training, and Generation
items.content: arXiv:2611.21983v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Language models are dynamical systems. A transformer is iterated over its layers, over the steps of its training and over the tokens it generates, and on each of these three clocks it shows behavior that nonlinear dynamics has studied for a century: fixed points, bifurcations, synchronization, chaos and noise-driven escape from potential wells. The two communities rarely meet, so this behavior is often rediscovered under new names. We build a bridge between them. To describe, we condense about 200 papers into the Three-Clock Dictionary, which maps fifteen concepts of nonlinear dynamics onto each clock and marks every correspondence as proved, measured or conjectured, and we show each concept in a mechanical system and in a language model side by side. To explain, we derive reduced-order models: the softmax is a Boltzmann distribution, gradient descent an Euler step on a nonlinear spring, a loss spike a ball thrown out of a stiff valley, attention on the circle a Kuramoto model, and a repetition loop a well that deepens while it is occupied. We then test these explanations on open language models, on a laptop CPU. Escape from repetition loops in GPT-2 and Pythia follows the Arrhenius law with the logit gap as the barrier, and the barrier deepens and then saturates, so the temperature needed to leave a loop falls like $1/\ln N$ with the generation length $N$ and rises with model size. Coherent text lives in a narrow window of temperatures, which a small reasoning model shares at its recommended temperature. Training makes each Pythia layer more expansive, and a small transformer trains at a multi-mode edge of stability. The third step, solving problems of language models, is still ahead: controllers derived from the escape analysis remove loops but do not yet beat the best fixed temperature. We state twelve open problems where nonlinear dynamics could get there.

Its value is primarily conceptual and integrative rather than presenting new results, which limits empirical impact but increases its usefulness as a reference.

items.title: Sample-efficient Personalization of Large Language Model Alignment with Multidimensional User Preference Data
items.content: arXiv:2611.22210v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Preference alignment has become a central tool to align large language models (LLMs) with human values and desired behavior, and its online variant can further advance their capabilities beyond what static data alone offer by repeatedly generating and labeling new responses with human feedback. But costly, time-consuming annotations limit its scalability, making sample efficiency essential, and existing methods typically seek to improve it by expanding coverage of the response space or selecting pairs with the highest uncertainty for comparison. Although they are effective, these methods quantify uncertainty from the perspective of the LLM, which may differ from the uncertainty perceived by the user: a pair can appear highly uncertain to the LLM even when past comparisons from the user already imply a clear ordering. In this paper, we propose multidimensional preference-guided online direct preference optimization (MPG-DPO), which leverages low-cost multidimensional evaluations from automated verifiers on the user historical comparisons to construct a personalized preference cone guiding response selection for online preference alignment. Specifically, it first discards responses that are confidently dominated under the estimated user preference, then selects two responses that are competitive under the retained preference cone yet exhibit the strongest unresolved disagreement. Theoretical analysis shows that, with high probability, the fraction of queries spent on cone-dominated responses vanishes as learning progresses. Experiments across multiple LLM families show that MPG-DPO outperforms strong contenders under matched query budgets.
items.author: Zhen-Yu Zhang, Jerry Huang, Gang Niu, Takashi Ishida, Masashi Sugiyama
items.summary: The authors improve sample efficiency of online LLM preference alignment by noting that LLM-perceived uncertainty differs from user-perceived uncertainty, and that user preferences are often multidimensional. They leverage multidimensional user preference data to select comparison pairs that are more informative from the user perspective, enabling personalized alignment with fewer annotations.
items.reasoning: Directly relevant to alignment scalability, a central bottleneck for LLM deployment, with a thoughtful reframing of active learning from the model uncertainty view to the user uncertainty view. Strong author team (Sugiyama lab and collaborators) and a clear path to practical impact in personalized RLHF.

items.title: Escaping Latent Traps by Remembering: Training-Free Episodic Kernel Repulsion for World-Model Planning
items.content: arXiv:2611.22470v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Latent world models plan towards a goal image by minimising the distance between predicted and goal latents. This distance is not geodesic: it has local minima, latent traps, behind walls, at corners and in dead ends, and memoryless receding-horizon replanning keeps the agent in them, revisiting states far from the goal. We propose Episodic Kernel Repulsion (EKR), a training-free cost term that penalises candidate plans by a top-$k$ Gaussian kernel to a novelty-gated memory of the latents the agent has actually visited, rescaled by the current base cost so that its strength is comparable across models. Across two JEPA world models and four benchmarks, EKR raises average success from 31.8% to 46.7% (LeWM) and from 54.7% to 64.0% (H-JEPA) with the same model, planner and budget. Same-memory counterfactuals show that, in most settings, EKR pushes plans away from visited states, in navigation, often at a higher base cost; stuck episodes and revisits drop accordingly. In seven of eight settings it matches or exceeds $4\times$ samples at $0.8$--$1.5\times$ compute. Without tuning, it transfers to DINO-WM with CEM: $+6.7$ and $+19.3$ points on official and longer-goal Wall tasks, and from 44.7% to 100.0% and from 21.0% to 32.0% on long-horizon PointMaze and Push-T.
items.author: Yican Zhao, Bolin Yang, Ruizhe Wang, Haiyang Guo, Fuji Yang, Bingo Wing-Kuen Ling, Zelin Zang
items.summary: The paper identifies latent traps, local minima in latent distance that strand world-model agents behind walls and in dead ends, and proposes Episodic Kernel Repulsion, a training-free cost term that penalizes revisiting latents stored in a novelty-gated episodic memory. Across two JEPA world models and four benchmarks, average planning success improves substantially, for example from 31.8 percent to 46.7 percent on LeWM. This is a clean, plug-in improvement for memoryless receding-horizon planning.
items.reasoning: Training-free methods with strong, consistent empirical gains across multiple world models and benchmarks are valuable and immediately usable. The idea of episodic memory-based repulsion is intuitive rather than deeply novel, but the diagnosis of latent traps is a genuine contribution to world-model planning.

items.title: Who Pays for Byzantine Robustness? Validity, Data-Share Dictatorships, and Fairness When Only a Few Hospitals Collaborate
items.content: arXiv:2611.22904v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Clinical federated learning (FL) collaborations typically connect only three to six hospitals, yet Byzantine-robust aggregation rules are designed and benchmarked on synthetic partitions across dozens of equal-sized clients. We conduct an empirical audit of eight standard aggregation rules: FedAvg, coordinate-wise median, trimmed mean, Krum, Multi-Krum, Bulyan, geometric median (GeoMed), and Centered Clipping (CC). We evaluate both unweighted and sample-size-weighted variants across three cross-silo medical datasets from the FLamby benchmark: Fed-Heart-Disease ($n = 4$ hospitals), Fed-TCGA-BRCA ($n = 6$ regions), and Fed-ISIC2019 ($n = 6$ centres). We execute 54,214 training runs across enumerated attacker coalitions ($f \in \{1, 2\}$) paired with exact-twin leave-out controls that decompose performance drops into honest data loss versus adversarial attack damage.   We report three findings. First, client-count validity checks fail to capture breakdown in skewed medical consortia: while $n = 6, f = 1$ satisfies every count condition except Bulyan's, assigning sample-size weights turns median and GeoMed into a clean-model dictatorship whenever a single hospital holds more than half the training data, and causes weighted median, GeoMed, and CC to collapse when that dominant centre attacks. Second, exact-twin leave-out controls reveal that when the largest hospital attacks, the apparent failure of count-based robust rules is predominantly caused by the loss of honest training data (7.5 to 10.4 points on ISIC) rather than adversarial perturbation (2.3 to 3.8 points on ISIC). Conversely, weight-dependent rules suffer large true attack damage (16.1 to 25.1 points on ISIC). Third, unweighted robust rules consistently discount whichever institution generates the most atypical parameter updates, penalizing the smallest hospital on Heart but penalizing larger institutions on TCGA and ISIC.

It reveals issues of validity, data-share dictatorships, and fairness that synthetic many-client benchmarks conceal. The work challenges standard robust-aggregation evaluation practice.

Findings that standard robustness methods misbehave with few unequal clients are practically important, though the contribution is empirical rather than methodological.

items.title: The Illusion of Grounding: Do Vision-Language Models Weigh Retrieved Text and Images Like an Ideal Observer?
items.content: arXiv:2611.23127v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Retrieval-augmented vision-language models (VLMs) answer from two sources of evidence that can each fail: the retrieved text can be wrong or noisy, and the image can be degraded or contradicted. We introduce GIB-200K, 200,000 image-question items built from COCO and Visual Genome, each expanded into controlled stress conditions: hard-negative retrieval noise (1-20 documents), visual ambiguity (Gaussian and motion blur, low-resource crops) and cross-modal conflict with counterfactual flip pairs. Instead of only measuring degradation, we ask how models combine the two modalities. From ideal Bayesian cue combination we derive a testable prediction that yields formal definitions of Knowledge Inertia (text over-weighted relative to the model's own image evidence) and Sensory Capture (the reverse), and we estimate the weights with a measurement-error-corrected regression whose recovery of known weights we verify. A counterfactual flip decomposition separates modality bias from concept priors, and a Grounding Illusion Score measures how much clean accuracy is not grounded in the image. We evaluate 4 open models on one frozen, seeded evaluation split of 2,000 GIB-200K items. All models are accurate on clean inputs (92.5%-94.2%) but adverse accuracy falls to 41.3%-59.9%. The two LLaVA models over-weight the text (Knowledge Inertia, w_T/w_I = 1.229 and 1.322), whereas InternVL3 favours the image (w_T/w_I = 0.680); between 34.8% and 71.4% of the clean answers that are correct are abandoned when the document lies. A training-free consistency check that compares the answer with and without retrieval trades coverage for accuracy under misleading documents, while falling back to the image fails when the image is heavily degraded. All per-instance outputs, code, and an audit that recomputes every reported open-model number are released.

items.title: Discovery of new antiviral agents through artificial intelligence: in vitro and in vivo results
items.content: arXiv:2611.22230v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: In this research, we employed a deep reinforcement learning (RL)-based molecule design platform to generate a diverse set of compounds targeting the neuraminidase (NA) of influenza A and B viruses. A total of 60291 compounds were generated, of which 86.5% displayed superior physicochemical properties compared to oseltamivir. After narrowing down the selection through computational filters, nine compounds with non-sialic acid-like structures were selected for in vitro experiments. We identified two compounds, DS-22-inf-009 and DS-22-inf-021 that effectively inhibited the NAs of both influenza A and B viruses (IAV and IBV), including H275Y mutant strains at low micromolar concentrations. Molecular dynamics simulations revealed a similar pattern of interaction with amino acid residues as oseltamivir. In cell-based assays, DS-22-inf-009 and DS-22-inf-021 inhibited IAV and IBV in a dose-dependent manner with EC50 values ranging from 0.29 uM to 2.31 uM. Furthermore, animal experiments showed that both DS-22-inf-009 and DS-22-inf-021 exerted antiviral activity in mice, conferring 65% and 85% protection from IAV (H1N1 pdm09), and 65% and 100% protection from IBV (Yamagata lineage), respectively. Thus, these findings demonstrate the potential of RL to generate compounds with promising antiviral properties.

Nine compounds were synthesized and tested, yielding two non-sialic-acid-like inhibitors effective against influenza A and B, including H275Y mutant strains, validated in vitro and in vivo.
items.reasoning: End-to-end AI-driven drug discovery with actual wet-lab, in vitro, and in vivo validation, which is far rarer than purely computational proposals. The demonstrated hit compounds against resistant influenza strains give this strong applied significance, though the RL methodology itself is standard.

Molecular dynamics simulations revealed a similar pattern of interaction with amino acid residues as oseltamivir. In cell-based assays, DS-22-inf-009 and DS-22-inf-021 inhibited IAV and IBV in a dose-dependent manner with EC50 values ranging from 0.29 uM to 2.31 uM. Furthermore, animal experiments showed that both DS-22-inf-009 and DS-22-inf-021 exerted antiviral activity in mice, conferring 65% and 85% protection from IAV (H1N1 pdm09), and 65% and 100% protection from IBV (Yamagata lineage), respectively. Thus, these findings demonstrate the potential of RL to generate compounds with promising antiviral properties.

items.title: Task Convergent Flow Matching for Generative Robotics
items.content: arXiv:2611.22609v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Successful manipulation requires the manipulated objects to progress toward a desired task outcome. Generative policies can produce plausible robot motions without ensuring this progress, allowing successive action chunks to stall or undo earlier changes to the scene. We introduce a task-centric inference-time refinement framework for flow matching policies that evaluates candidate action chunks through parallel physics-based rollouts and searches for motions satisfying sufficient conditions for task convergence. Task-level performance funnels bound temporary regressions while requiring net progress over each chunk. We establish sufficient conditions under which repeated funnel satisfaction yields convergence throughout execution, and use interval-wise Lipschitz bounds to verify continuous-time funnel satisfaction from sampled rollouts. To accommodate contact-rich hybrid dynamics, we refine the flow's source seeds using derivative-free Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy (CMA-ES), constrained to radial quantile bands of the source distribution to help retain the learned motion prior. This formulation supports both Euclidean and pose-valued Riemannian Flow Matching (RMFM) policies. On PushT and three-cube stacking, refinement raises success from 31.3% to 88.5% and from 77.0% to 86.0%. On PushT, whose coverage score responds continuously to the motion of the block, a learned funnel lowers the average maximum loss of achieved progress by 19% relative to constraining the endpoint of each chunk alone, at a similar success rate. With the radial band, 11.3% of the executed motion windows are out of distribution, a rate within the range of held-out demonstrations, compared with 34.1% for an unconstrained search.

items.title: Spool: Low-Latency Streaming Inference for Hybrid Vision-Language Models
items.content: arXiv:2611.23228v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Applications such as visual accessibility agents and robotics require answering questions about recent video content promptly, over a bounded window of past frames (e.g., the last two minutes). Hybrid vision-language models (VLMs), which interleave attention with linear recurrent layers such as Gated DeltaNet (GDN), are attractive for this setting, but maintaining a sliding window is expensive. The reason is that recurrent layers combine all past frames into a shared state, so expiring old frames normally requires re-running the entire window through the model. We observe that the recurrent update is affine in the state with input-dependent coefficients, so the effect of each frame can be captured as a transformation that composes associatively. We present Spool, a training-free framework that caches per-frame state transformations and composes them efficiently as the window advances, removing expired frames from each recurrent layer's state without replaying frames through the backbone. Removal is exact within each layer; as with key-value eviction in attention, expired frames can retain residual influence through the cached inputs computed by earlier layers. We design a dedicated data structure and GPU kernels to achieve low caching and composition overhead. Across five open-source hybrid VLMs and four video reasoning benchmarks, Spool achieves the lowest p95 time-to-first-token in all 20 model-benchmark tests, reducing it by a geometric mean of $6.6\times$ over the faster of two recent vLLM baselines, while improving accuracy by 2.3 percentage points on average.
