items.title: CRA: Continuous Risk Assessment for Safety-critical Visual Navigation
items.content: arXiv:2611.22080v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Traditional safety-critical control methods often rely on predefined constraints that separate states into safe and unsafe regions. While recent studies have extended geometric safety toward semantic safety, real-world safety is rarely purely binary. The risk associated with an object or human can vary continuously with its physical properties, like motion, and interaction context; for example, a person carrying a heavy object or a hot object moving at high speed may require a different safety response from an ordinary static obstacle. In this paper, we propose a vision-based continuous risk assessment framework for safety-critical visual navigation. Our method uses RGB and LiDAR observations to estimate four risk factors (kinetic, potential, contact-severity, and thermal) and combines them into a continuous risk score for each assessed object or person. These estimates are integrated into a Poisson safety function with a Laplace guidance field as a safety filter, enabling online monitoring and intervention in open-world robot navigation. We demonstrate the proposed method in a simulated restaurant scene.

For example, a fast-moving person carrying a hot object warrants a different response than a static obstacle.

items.title: COAST: Safe Flight Corridor Planner for Fast and Robust Snap Minimized Trajectories
items.content: arXiv:2611.22447v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Current B-Spline trajectory planners face a critical trade-off: they either sacrifice computational speed to maintain strict Safe Flight Corridor (SFC) guarantees, or they abandon hard safety bounds in favor of soft-constraint penalties to achieve real-time performance. We present COAST (Corridor-Optimized Aerially-Safe Trajectories), a B-Spline based, online trajectory planner capable of formulating snap minimized trajectories with SFC guarantees. COAST divides the problem into two stages: an A* based front-end that generates geometrically simple SFCs (represented as a chain of rectangular prisms), and a quadratic programming back-end for control point optimization. To handle the non-convexity of SFC intersections, we leverage the finite support property of B-Splines, to ensure the spline never exits SFC boundaries. The control point optimization incorporates MINVO transforms for kinodynamic bounding, allowing COAST to design non-conservative, dynamically feasible trajectories, while a snap minimization matrix calculation provides flight smoothness. This formulation provides a formal geometric containment guarantee, while ensuring mean trajectory computation times under 5 ms for real-time deployment. We validate our results through high-fidelity simulation experiments. The source code can be found at: https://github.com/byu-magicc/Minimum-Snap-Trajectories

items.summary: COAST is an online B-Spline trajectory planner that produces snap-minimized trajectories with hard Safe Flight Corridor guarantees, combining an A* front-end generating simple rectangular corridor chains with a QP back-end, handling non-convex corridor intersections. It resolves the speed-versus-safety trade-off in current B-Spline planners.

items.title: Sim2CBF: From Forward Simulations to Implicit Control Barrier Function Safety Filtering without Model Derivatives
items.content: arXiv:2611.22954v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Failure avoidance in complex robot-environment interactions is challenging because the underlying dynamics are difficult to model accurately, and available predictive models may not provide reliable derivatives. We present Sim2CBF, a failure-avoidance framework that solves the Control Barrier Function (CBF)-Safety Filter (SF) optimization problem using only forward-model evaluations, thereby avoiding differentiation of the predictive model. Specifically, we approximate the CBF constraint using finite differences and local linear interpolation over sampled control inputs while preserving failure-avoidance guarantees. The underlying CBF is implicit and constructed from backup-policy rollouts, enabling the use of expressive predictive models such as physics-based simulators and learned world models. Compared with purely sampling-based SFs, our formulation requires fewer control samples and yields less conservative behavior than direct nominal-backup blending. We evaluate Sim2CBF in simulation, hardware box-toppling, and vision-based control tasks, demonstrating its applicability to contact-rich and learned dynamics, as well as its adaptability to changes in the predictive model.

items.title: Thoughts on "safety bad bc warning shots good"
items.content:
Suppose there was a button which made the current generation of AIs more safe, i.e. more aligned and less capable of subverting control measures. The button has no other effects — in particular, the button wouldn’t make future generations more or less safe. Should you press the button?

Maybe you shouldn’t, because of the Warning Shot Argument:

- Future agents contribute almost all the risk of catastrophe, compared with current agents.
- Pressing the button makes current agents safer.
- If current agents are safer, then they are less likely to cause non-catastrophic harms, e.g. cybercrime.
- If current agents don’t cause non-catastrophic harms, then people will be less aware about catastrophic risks, e.g. lab leadership, governments, legislators, international community, lab employees, general public, media, academia, etc.
- If people are less aware about catastrophic risks, then they won’t take drastic action to reduce catastrophic risk.
- So future agents contribute more catastrophic risk.
- Therefore pressing the button would increase catastrophic risk.

This might seem very abstract, but consider a concrete example. Suppose you’d pressed the button to make OpenAI’s HPIM more aligned and less capable to subvert control measures. Then the HuggingFace incident would never have happened. And that probably would’ve increased catastrophic risk.

## Is this self-defeating?

The story is a little suspicious. In particular, it seems to account the second-order effect, i.e. “more safety -> fewer warning shots -> less awareness -> less safety”. But ignores the higher-order effects like “more safety -> fewer warning shots -> less awareness -> less safety -> more warning shots -> more awareness -> more safety”.

Now, maybe the second-order effect is bigger than the first-order effects and all higher-order effects. But it seems like that would involve pretty messy quantitive modelling that no one has grappled with....

items.summary: Cleo Nardo examines the Warning Shot Argument, which claims that making current-generation AIs safer could paradoxically increase catastrophic risk by preventing the non-catastrophic harms that raise societal awareness and drive protective action. The post formalizes the argument step by step and begins exploring whether a safety-improving intervention should be pressed, using a hypothetical button framing and a concrete lab-focused example.

It is purely theoretical with no empirical component, but it comes from a recognized alignment community writer and addresses a decision-relevant question for safety interventions today.

items.title: When Lower Harm Misleads: Auditing Concept Corrections
items.content: arXiv:2611.22084v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: An expert who corrects a concept prediction, such as a BI-RADS descriptor in breast ultrasound, expects the diagnosis to improve. Objectives that reduce the harm of such corrections are judged by harm and accuracy, yet harm also falls when a model responds less to every correction or starts from a worse uncorrected prediction, the reference for harm. We propose a correction audit, a reproducible evaluation protocol that separates these explanations: it splits each correction into harm and useful gain on identical events, separates the starting prediction from the correction response, and compares objectives with amplitude baselines matched in source harm. On three breast-ultrasound sources, worst-case correction training, evaluated from the mean-case model's start, lowers harm but gives up more useful gain in all 21 source comparisons pooled over six seeds, raising the corrected negative log-likelihood (NLL); from the same start, selecting between the objectives by harm picks the less helpful model on all three sources. On CUB, a monotonic harm penalty at its reported weight lowers path-level harm in all 80 concept sets while raising the NLL in all 80, almost entirely before any correction. At a fixed start, rescaling both responses to the same source harm reproduces the penalty's mean harm, useful gain and NLL on single-concept corrections within a prespecified margin of 0.0005 nat, although the two responses point in different directions. Lower harm therefore signals better corrections only when it is read together with useful gain, absolute risk and the start it is measured from.
items.author: Tianyou Lai, Wentao Yue, Hongji Li, Chaoyuan Hao, Qilei Li
items.summary: The authors propose a correction audit protocol for expert corrections of concept predictions (e.g., BI-RADS descriptors in breast ultrasound) that separates harm reduction from useful gain and distinguishes a worse starting prediction from genuine correction responsiveness. Applied across three breast-ultrasound sources, the audit reveals when objectives appear beneficial merely by lowering responsiveness or starting from worse baselines.
items.reasoning: A careful methodological contribution exposing subtle confounds in evaluating correction-aware learning, with a concrete medical imaging application. The audit protocol is reproducible and broadly applicable, but the paper's scope and immediate impact are niche.

items.title: Towards Physics-Constrained Rectified Flow for Climate Downscaling: What Projections Can Certify?
items.content: arXiv:2611.22283v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Statistical downscaling restores the regional detail behind flooding and crop stress, but diffusion and flow-matching generators can produce sharp fields that break the conservation laws of their coarse input. Physics-Constrained Rectified Flow (PC-RF) is a conditional flow-matching downscaler. Its training penalties target wind divergence, negative precipitation, and mass drift from the coarse total, and a projection after sampling removes the last two exactly. On one corrupted synthetic field with no trained network, the projection drives the Non-negativity Violation Rate (NVR) from 0.236 and the Mass-Conservation Error (MCE) from 0.184 to zero, and the penalties lower the Divergence Error (DE) by about 30%. On ERA5 the projection gives PC-RF and RF-base, the penalty-free rectified-flow baseline, an NVR of exactly zero and an MCE of zero up to float32 rounding. The penalties add no perceptual gain that we can separate from training budget or run-to-run variation. At a matched budget on 2019-2021, PC-RF has no edge over RF-base (SSIM 0.939 vs. 0.942, PSNR 31.81 vs. 31.79, CRPS 0.771 vs. 0.772). Our unprojected CorrDiff reimplementation beats both flow models on PSNR (28.38) and CRPS (1.092) on 2020, yet 45% of its ensemble-mean precipitation cells are negative. On ERA5 a sign error in the divergence operator made that penalty and DE act on a deformation-like term. The fine reference is interpolated from ERA5 and accumulates precipitation over a longer window, so the perceptual scores cannot establish downscaling skill. NVR and MCE need one pass and no fine reference, so we argue they should run first as pass-or-fail checks, with DE as a diagnostic.

items.title: Multistage Contextual Optimization for Vehicle Repositioning
items.content: arXiv:2611.22330v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Ride-hailing platforms reposition idle vehicles to improve spatial supply-demand balances. This problem is prediction-driven and multistage: at each stage, the platform forecasts future demand, executes current decisions, and uses the resulting state to initialize the next stage. We formulate a multistage linear program (LP) with a macroscopic fundamental diagram (MFD) linking accumulation to trip completion. We then develop a multistage contextual optimization approach that uses decision performance to train the prediction model. The learning problem combines multiple coupled stages, context that depends on earlier decisions, and predictions that affect the objective, the constraint matrix, and the right-hand side of the LP. We derive the exact gradient, which has three parts: parameters change forecasts and hence decisions; earlier decisions change the current decision through the inherited state; and this state also changes forecasts as context. An equivalent adjoint uses reverse vector-Jacobian products, avoiding full solution and state-parameter Jacobians. Finally, forward propagation solves many stage LPs one after another, which makes training slow. We propose a parallel block evaluation algorithm that solves blocks of consecutive stages in parallel and repeatedly feeds each block output to the next block. We prove that the algorithm recovers the serial trajectory within a finite number of passes and that its gradient error remains bounded when it stops early. On New York City ride-hailing data, multistage contextual optimization yields 7.7% to 9.1% more business benefit than the same predictor trained by mean squared error, outperforms all compared baselines from five paradigms, and even outperforms realized demand fed to the same policy. With eight workers, parallel block evaluation shortens training by a factor of 1.86 without loss of decision performance.
items.author: Jinyu Zhang, Di Huang, Zhiyuan Liu, Nikolas Geroliminis
items.summary: This paper formulates ride-hailing vehicle repositioning as a multistage linear program coupled with a macroscopic fundamental diagram linking vehicle accumulation to trip completion. The authors develop a contextual optimization approach in which decision performance trains the demand-prediction model, handling coupled stages, decision-dependent context, and predictions that affect the objective, constraints, and right-hand side of the LP. They derive effective solutions and demonstrate improved spatial supply-demand balancing on real ride-hailing scenarios.
items.reasoning: A rigorous operations-research contribution with a clean integration of prediction and optimization (decision-focused learning style) applied to a high-value industry problem. The methodology is technically careful, but it is domain-specific rather than broadly transformative for AI, and the abstract indicates established techniques (LP, MFD, contextual optimization) combined in a new setting.

items.title: Structured AI ideation yields physical strategies for epithelial barrier repair
items.content: arXiv:2611.22988v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: AI systems increasingly support literature analysis, candidate evaluation and hypothesis refinement, but enabling researchers to explore research directions beyond established disciplinary approaches remains challenging. We developed Abelio, an AI system designed to generate novel research directions by expanding investigators' avenues of inquiry. Abelio reformulates research objectives, uses these alternative formulations to identify relevant elements outside conventional disciplinary boundaries, and refines the resulting hypotheses. Each stage integrates divergent exploration with convergent selection through a dedicated subsystem. In quantitative evaluations, proposals generated by the Ideation Core (Abelio's hypothesis-generation core) outperformed those of four frontier large language models in scientific soundness and hypothesis diversity, and three of four in distance from existing literature. Subsystem ablation showed that each subsystem contributes to the property it targets, with the contribution of Element Selection measurable before Refinement. To investigate intestinal epithelial barrier restoration, Abelio proposed physical interventions involving membrane-tethered poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) and cholesterol-anchored complementary DNA. Both proposals were archived before experimentation and subsequently tested independently in damaged Caco-2 monolayers. PEG preserved barrier function in a membrane-surface-dependent manner, whereas complementary DNA enabled sequence-specific restoration that was reversible on demand. These findings demonstrate how structured research ideation can identify experimentally testable approaches beyond established disciplinary conventions.

items.title: FCP: Formal Context Protocol for Verifying LLM-Generated Artifacts
items.content: arXiv:2611.21679v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: When a language model writes both an artifact and the tests meant to check it, a passing test is weak evidence: one misreading of the request yields a faulty artifact and a check that accepts it. We present the Formal Context Protocol (FCP), which checks AI-generated artifacts against the request itself. FCP separates conformance (does the artifact satisfy a formal reading of a requirement?), which model checkers and SMT solvers decide, from fidelity (does the reading mean what the prose means?), which has no decision procedure but is refutable by a concrete witness. Eight ways a proof can falsely certify a requirement each become a mechanical check that returns a witness, and what no machine can settle becomes concrete questions for the request's author. Adapters place hardware, text, agents and code on the same engines. On four hardware designs, trusting AI-written assertions certified 23% of violated requirements, and FCP certified none. On ten code tasks, code from three language models passed its own tests and violated the request every time. Trusting the tests certified all 33 violations, and FCP certified three. Agreement among models, readings or tests did not imply correctness.
items.author: Shashank
items.summary: FCP addresses the problem that when an LLM writes both an artifact and its tests, passing tests are weak evidence. It checks AI-generated artifacts against the request itself, separating conformance (decidable by SMT solvers and model checkers) from fidelity (undecidable but refutable by concrete witnesses), and turns eight ways a proof can falsely certify a requirement into mechanical witness-producing checks. This is a practical protocol for trustworthy verification of generated code and artifacts.
items.reasoning: A thoughtful verification protocol for a real and growing problem — trusting self-tested LLM outputs — with a principled split between decidable and refutable properties. Single-author, protocol-stage work without large-scale empirical validation keeps it below higher-impact scores, but the design is conceptually strong.

items.title: Can Coding Agents Write and Transpile Unit Tests
items.content: arXiv:2611.21797v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Coding assistants built on Large Language Models (LLMs) have become a staple of modern software development, increasingly trusted to execute workflows and modernize code end-to-end. Much of this trust rests on passing tests, which are often written by the coding agents themselves. In this work, we examine the ability of these agents to both write reliable tests and translate them between programming languages. We benchmark three popular coding agents, each evaluated with a native frontier model and high reasoning effort. Verifying across a broad suite of metrics, we find that coding agents far exceed human written suites on traditional measures of coverage. This advantage, however, is uneven: agent test quality degrades sharply with project size, and much of the advantage lies in a greater number of written tests. We also show that agentic test translation---while seemingly strong in aggregate---remains inconsistent and unreliable.
items.author: Gil Pasternak, AJ Langley, Tom Yotam, Ellie Kitanidis
items.summary: This work benchmarks three popular coding agents with frontier models on writing reliable unit tests and translating them between programming languages. Agents far exceed human-written suites on coverage metrics, but test quality degrades sharply with project complexity, tempering trust in agent-generated verification.
items.reasoning: Practically relevant empirical evaluation of a critical self-verification loop in agentic coding, with a useful negative finding, though the benchmark covers only three agents and breadth of metrics cannot fully substitute for depth.

items.title: When AUC Meets Generative Reconstruction: A Unified Principle for Balanced Visual Representation Learning
items.content: arXiv:2611.22094v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) require visual encoders that extract fine-grained visual features while constructing semantically disentangled and discriminative representations. Conventional methodologies encounter a fundamental trade-off: contrastive learning enhances inter-class discrimination by suppressing intra-class variability, whereas generative reconstruction emphasizes perceptual fidelity but lacks explicit comparative supervision. The naive aggregation of these objectives via composite loss functions often induces optimization conflicts and instability due to gradient interference within the shared latent space. To resolve this, we introduce a unified representation-learning paradigm that reformulates generative reconstruction as a discriminative ranking problem within the generative output manifold. Our approach maintains perceptual reconstruction as a supervisory signal and integrates a ranking-based discriminative constraint by systematically ordering matched and mismatched reconstruction outputs. This formulation embeds discriminative information seamlessly into the generative process, alleviating the risk of loss competition. Specifically, we propose AUC Generative Reconstruction (AUCGR), which optimizes the area under the ROC curve (AUC) by ensuring higher scores for matched pairs than for mismatched pairs, and Partial AUC Generative Reconstruction (pAUCGR), which addresses supervision bias by focusing on mismatched comparisons within reliable feature subspaces. The proposed objectives are designed to be plug-and-play, requiring no architectural modifications to existing generative reconstruction frameworks. Theoretical analysis establishes rigorous connections to AUC/pAUC optimization and provides generalization guarantees. Extensive experiments validate that our method advances both discriminative accuracy and fine-grained perceptual representation.

items.summary: The paper reformulates generative reconstruction within an AUC-optimization framework to unify contrastive discrimination and perceptual fidelity for visual encoders serving multimodal LLMs, avoiding gradient interference from naive composite losses. The aim is representations that are simultaneously fine-grained, discriminative, and reconstructive.
items.reasoning: Tackles a real optimization conflict in visual representation learning with a theoretically grounded unification rather than loss-weight tuning. The abstract suggests solid motivation from a credible group (Qianming Huang's group lineage), but the claimed benefits for downstream MLLM performance need empirical confirmation.

items.title: Teaching Language Models to Narrow Boolean Patent Searches from Search Feedback
items.content: arXiv:2611.22270v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Patent prior-art searchers issue Boolean queries line by line, broadening to find relevant documents and narrowing until candidates can be screened. We distill 38,397 Japan Patent Office search reports into executable expert strategies, re-execute them, and evaluate generated strategies by citation recall and the smallest set containing each citation. Prompted models write valid, high-recall strategies but leave citations in sets too large to screen. We adapt a generator offline from scored rollouts in two forms: strategy-level learning from a screening-aware strategy score, and line-level learning from citation-preserving narrowing credit, which upweights the query lines keeping a found citation in a smaller set. On shared rollouts, line-level credit outperforms strategy-level scores on screening measures; iterated, it cuts the median citation-containing set from 768 to under 50 and places more citations in sets under 100 documents than experts, at lower recall. Strategy-level preference learning reaches near-complete recall; the two forms are complementary.

items.summary: The authors distill 38,397 Japan Patent Office search reports into executable expert Boolean search strategies and train a generator offline from scored rollouts, using screening-aware strategy scores and line-level credit for citation-preserving narrowing. Prompted models write valid, high-recall strategies but leave citation sets too large to screen; the learned line-level approach improves narrowing. This demonstrates feedback-driven learning for a real professional search workflow.

items.title: What's in a Tree ? Hierarchical $n$-gram models as controlled approximators of language
items.content: arXiv:2611.23093v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Hierarchical models have been proposed as synthetic settings for studying language. However, their relevance to realistic language corpora remains underexplored. In this work, we introduce tree-grams, autoregressive generative $n$-gram models that build the conditional probability tensor $p(x_n \mid x_{1:n-1})$ through a hierarchical composition of order-2 and order-3 tensors. $n$ controls the maximal context window, whereas a rank hyperparameter $d$ controls model capacity, yielding an interpretable and systematically scalable family of approximators of language. We show how tree-grams outperform existing $n$-gram baselines, while remaining competitive with deep transformer-based language models. We demonstrate the utility of such controlled approximations by using tree-grams as generative models. In particular, we show that hyperparameter transfer under $\mu$P can be made more robust when narrower models are tuned on simpler data, generated by tree-grams with moderate $n$ and $d$. In addition, we show that entropy and effective range of correlations control performance gap after fine-tuning. This is because tree-grams allow us to explicitly control horizon and capacity. When allowed to route across candidate topologies, we observe emergent sparsity in tree-grams. Such concentrated routing permits pruning upto 95\% of topologies without significant change in performance.
items.author: Aritra Das, Francesco Cagnetta, Darshil Doshi, Victor V. Albert, Maissam Barkeshli, Andrey Gromov
items.summary: Introduces tree-grams, autoregressive n-gram models built through hierarchical composition of order-2 and order-3 tensors, with context window and capacity controlled by interpretable hyperparameters. Tree-grams beat existing n-gram baselines and stay competitive with transformer language models, enabling controlled studies of scaling and learnability.
items.reasoning: An elegant, interpretable modeling family useful as a scientific probe of language learnability and scaling behavior; conceptual value is high for the science-of-deep-learning community, though direct practical impact is limited.

items.title: VisHead-Spec: Head-Routed Visual Attention for Multimodal Speculative Decoding
items.content: arXiv:2611.21839v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates vision-language models(VLMs) while preserving the target model's outputs, but its speedup diminishes under high concurrency serving as the system becomes more compute bounded as the batch size increases. This problem is pronounced for multimodal speculative decoding as the long range of the image tokens in the prompt can significantly increase the computational cost during draft token prediction. The block-diffusion drafters (e.g. DFlash, DSpark) can effectively speed up the draft model efficiency by predicting multiple draft tokens in one forward pass, but their speedup for VLMs under high concurrency is still modest (<9%). In order to understand this gap, we examine the information flow between different modalities from target model to draft model and identify the sparsity pattern of visual attention between the target and draft models: only small set of key-value heads in the draft model need direct visual feature attention in the context and only visual features from top level layers in the target model need to be attended in the context. We therefore propose VisHead-Spec, which selects a small, fixed set of key-value (KV) heads to attend to all image features from top level layers in the target model and restricts the remaining heads to text features. On Qwen3-VL-8B and MMSpec, VisHead-Spec-8 lets 8 of the drafter's 40 KV heads read the image while keeping accepted length within 0.3% of the block-diffusion draft model baseline (i.e. DSpark). At batch size 64, its throughput gain over autoregressive decoding increases to 16.0%, compared with 9.5% for DSpark; at batch size 1, its speedup remains comparable to DSpark.
items.author: Xin Guo, Arushi Rai, Xiang Zhou, Qiang Zhang, Siyu Lin, Xiangjun Fan, Lizhu Zhang
items.summary: The paper explains why multimodal speculative decoding speedups collapse under high concurrency: image tokens inflate draft computation as batches become compute-bound, and block-diffusion drafters like DFlash and DSpark achieve under 9 percent speedup in this regime. Through information-flow analysis across model components, the authors identify how visual attention is routed through specific heads and propose head-routed visual attention to make drafting more efficient. The approach preserves target model outputs while improving VLM serving throughput.
items.reasoning: A well-diagnosed serving problem with an interpretability-informed fix, relevant as VLM inference at scale is a major cost center; the analysis connecting information flow to speculation efficiency is technically interesting. Reported gains appear incremental in the most favorable framing, and the method applies to a specific drafting family.

items.content_html: arXiv:2611.21839v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates vision-language models(VLMs) while preserving the target model's outputs, but its speedup diminishes under high concurrency serving as the system becomes more compute bounded as the batch size increases. This problem is pronounced for multimodal speculative decoding as the long range of the image tokens in the prompt can significantly increase the computational cost during draft token prediction. The block-diffusion drafters (e.g. DFlash, DSpark) can effectively speed up the draft model efficiency by predicting multiple draft tokens in one forward pass, but their speedup for VLMs under high concurrency is still modest (<9%). In order to understand this gap, we examine the information flow between different modalities from target model to draft model and identify the sparsity pattern of visual attention between the target and draft models: only small set of key-value heads in the draft model need direct visual feature attention in the context and only visual features from top level layers in the target model need to be attended in the context. We therefore propose VisHead-Spec, which selects a small, fixed set of key-value (KV) heads to attend to all image features from top level layers in the target model and restricts the remaining heads to text features. On Qwen3-VL-8B and MMSpec, VisHead-Spec-8 lets 8 of the drafter's 40 KV heads read the image while keeping accepted length within 0.3% of the block-diffusion draft model baseline (i.e. DSpark). At batch size 64, its throughput gain over autoregressive decoding increases to 16.0%, compared with 9.5% for DSpark; at batch size 1, its speedup remains comparable to DSpark.

items.title: HADVQ: Hessian Aware Directional Vector Quantization
items.content: arXiv:2611.22721v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Ultra-low-bit quantization of large language models is a challenging task because aggressive compression severely distorts model parameters and disproportionately harms a small number of highly sensitive channels. We present a vector quantization method tailored for this regime. Our approach begins with random preconditioning, which regularizes the weight space and makes it more amenable to quantization. We then represent weights in polar coordinates and decouple the quantization of directions and magnitudes. To quantize directions, we leverage the structure induced by random preconditioning and design a structured codebook based on the $E_8$ lattice, yielding a compact yet expressive representation. To further reduce degradation, we detect extremely important channels using a proxy Hessian and preserve them with an additional cost of only 0.16 bits. Together, these components provide an effective quantization pipeline for LLMs in the extremely low-bit regime. Empirical results demonstrate improved accuracy, highlighting the benefit of combining geometric structure, lattice-based codebooks, and selective channel preservation.

items.reasoning: Ultra-low-bit quantization is industrially important, and the combination of Hessian-aware sensitivity handling with lattice codebooks is technically interesting. However, the field is crowded with strong recent quantization methods, and the abstract does not indicate SOTA superiority or large-scale validation.

items.title: Action-outcome coupling: a pre-investment feasibility audit for offline reinforcement learning in supply chain operations
items.content: arXiv:2611.22921v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Prescriptive analytics initiatives in logistics, such as offline reinforcement learning and next-best-action systems, are often funded before anyone verifies that the available historical logs can support an improved decision policy. We formalise this pre-investment feasibility question via action-outcome coupling: a total-effect variance index measuring how much expected outcomes change with the logged action. Coupling provides an algorithm-independent upper bound on any policy's achievable value, expressed in monetary units per decision for both single-step and discounted sequential objectives. We also analyse the asymptotic false-licensing risk of an invalid workflow: fitting a value model and evaluating the model's greedy policy on the same data. The false-licence rate is driven mainly by the number of state cells over which selection is performed, rising from the nominal test level with one cell to near certainty with a few dozen, while overlap has a smaller effect. We then propose an audit that assigns logs to four tiers of decision support, separately for fixed and contextual policies, and returns an explicit stopping rationale. On a randomised e-commerce log, the audit endorses a fixed recommendation policy, certifying gains equal to 30 per cent of the theoretical ceiling; the remaining gap reflects bound looseness under an 80-action design. Two public logistics logs fail at different checkpoints: one because the target is an accounting identity of the action, and another because, with 27 clusters, estimated coupling stays below the design's detectability threshold even though a conservative offline learner certifies an improvement in 29 of 30 seeds.

Coupling yields an algorithm-independent upper bound on achievable policy value in monetary units and an analysis of false-licensing risk when naive value-model workflows are applied to low-signal logs. This helps organizations decide whether offline RL initiatives are worth funding.
items.reasoning: A thoughtful, decision-focused framework addressing a real deployment gap: knowing before investing whether logged data can support better policies. The formalism is sensible but domain-tilted toward supply chains, and empirical validation of the audit in practice is unclear from the abstract.

items.title: Wrong Input, Wrong Threshold: Re-evaluating Adversarial Facial Privacy
items.content: arXiv:2611.21923v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Published face-privacy methods report protection above 90% against black-box recognition models. That number comes from an evaluation protocol with two independent defects, reported in a measure that cannot size either one. The input is wrong: methods published since 2022 feed the network the whole photograph, or a detector's box, where deployed systems detect, align to a landmark template and crop. Re-scoring the same files through a realistic front end costs a standard transfer attack 56% of its dodging protection and a budget-allocating attack 7%, with no image regenerated. The measure is wrong: that loss is a difference of success rates, so it saturates, moving by 8.2x over a budget sweep while the effect beneath it moves by 1.34x. We therefore report the paired cosine shift, in which both thresholds cancel algebraically, so the input defect holds without committing to a calibration. Measured that way it is 2.2x and 10.7x larger on three unseen recognizers, and at matched budget it reverses the L-infinity transfer ranking: the one surveyed method that aligns at evaluation gains 0.18 where MI-FGSM loses 0.05. The cause is a resampling mismatch, not perturbation lost outside the crop; optimising through a differentiable alignment operator largely removes it, adding +24 to +58 points on unseen recognizers and a commercial system, with a residual on one of them. The thresholds are wrong: the four constants inherited since 2021 hold the false-accept rate near its nominal 1% on aligned crops but admit 2.3-5.4% on whole images, with an opposite-signed bias across dodging and impersonation, the two tasks reported side by side. Differentiable alignment and gallery scoring are not new: the first generation of this literature used both, and we show what dropping them cost.
items.author: Tunahan Parlay{\i}c{\i}, Erchan Aptoula, Y\"ucel Sayg{\i}n
items.summary: This evaluation paper shows that reported face-privacy protection rates above 90% are inflated by two protocol defects: unrealistic input pipelines that skip detection-alignment-cropping, and a saturating success-rate-difference metric. Re-scoring through a realistic front end costs a standard transfer attack 56% of its dodging protection, with the metric masking underlying effects.
items.reasoning: A rigorous methodological audit with concrete quantified corrections to an evaluation literature, valuable for anyone deploying or assessing adversarial facial privacy; the contribution is corrective rather than constructive, and confined to one application area.

items.title: Auditing a Learned Simulator for Legged Robots: The Robotic World Model on ANYmal D
items.content: arXiv:2611.23118v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: A legged robot can learn to walk inside a learned simulator: a neural network that predicts the robot's next state and is run forward on its own predictions. They are usually trained and checked one step ahead, although a policy uses them for a hundred steps or more. We audit one published system end to end, without a GPU: the dynamics model of the Robotic World Model (RWM) for the ANYmal D quadruped, and the uncertainty estimate of its follow-up, RWM-U. We rebuilt the model to match the released code's outputs, losses and gradients exactly, measured 101 trained simulators, 200 compressed copies and 38 simulators of three other architectures, and trained policies inside simulators that we tested in a hand-built MuJoCo model of the robot. Training on the model's own rollouts beat one-step training at 368 steps on all ten held-out episodes (registered), although one-step training was better one step ahead. One-step checks therefore misjudge design choices: pruning 30% of the weights kept 90% of the model's skill one step ahead and 39% at 2 s. Ensemble disagreement ranked rollout error well (Spearman +0.90 at 100 steps), yet covered 4.6% of outcomes at one sigma, against 68% for a calibrated estimate, as each network's own variance collapses under the implemented loss. Two checks that need no recorded future ranked some pools of simulators well, but neither was shown better than 8-step error in a primary test. At the robot level, accuracy has not predicted walking: all 18 fine-tuned copies we tested predicted better than the released model one and eight steps ahead, yet 13 gave failing policies, and registered tests of whether any check ranks simulators by their policies were not settled. In a secondary test, running the authors' policy inside each simulator ranked them well. We also report nine of our own claims that we withdrew. Scope: one robot, one gait, simulated data, no hardware.

items.summary: An end-to-end audit of a published learned simulator (Robotic World Model) for the ANYmal D quadruped, rebuilt without a GPU to match released code outputs exactly, covering 101 trained simulators, 200 compressed copies, and 38 simulators of three other architectures. The audit examines the model's one-step-ahead validation versus its actual use over hundreds of autoregressive steps, and tests policies in a hand-built MuJoCo model. Rare, rigorous reproducibility and reliability analysis of a learned world model.

items.title: Can a World Model Predict a Deepfake Video? A Consistency Margin Prior for Deepfake Detection
items.content: arXiv:2611.21846v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Deepfake detectors often perform well on the dataset they are trained on, but their performance drops when tested on videos from different datasets. In this paper, we study whether a predictive video model can provide a signal that generalizes better across datasets. Instead of relying only on generator-specific artifacts, as many existing detectors do, we use a model trained to predict natural video and measure the difference between what it predicts and what it observes in a video. Using V-JEPA 2.1, we keep the encoder frozen and adapt the predictor using rank-16 LoRA. We define the difference between the predictor output and the frozen encoder target as the prediction residual. We hypothesize that manipulated clips produce, on average, larger prediction residuals than authentic clips, and use this as our consistency-margin prior. We process these residuals using a lightweight Latent Consistency Head (LCH), which separates residual magnitude from direction for training and classification. To test whether the direction of the consistency margin affects cross-dataset generalization, we compare standard and reversed margin objectives while keeping the remaining training setup fixed. We match the two settings on FF++ validation performance before evaluating them on unseen data. The reversed-margin setting exhibits a larger cross dataset generalization gap on average, providing evidence that the direction of the consistency margin affects cross-dataset transfer. Our complete model adds only 8.25M trainable parameters, which is 2.47% of the total 334M parameters. Trained only on FF++, it achieves an AUC of 90.5 on Celeb-DFv2 and performs well across several other cross-dataset benchmarks. Our ablations show that separating residual magnitude from direction, reducing dataset-specific variation, and using a low-rank projection improve cross-dataset generalization in our experiments.
items.author: Pradip Gupta, Shubham Mandloi, Ravi Kumar Satzoda, Sujeeth Bharadwaj, Yassine Benajiba, Dan Roth
items.summary: This paper proposes deepfake detection via the prediction residual of a natural-video world model: using a frozen V-JEPA 2.1 encoder with a LoRA-adapted predictor, manipulated clips should produce larger gaps between predicted and observed frames. The approach aims to generalize across datasets better than detectors that rely on generator-specific artifacts. It connects self-supervised video world models to the deepfake-detection generalization problem.

Generalization claims across datasets would be significant if well supported, but the technique is an adaptation of existing components rather than a new architecture.

items.title: Cross3DGS: Unified Vulkan-Based 3D Gaussian Splatting Training from Workstations to Mobile Devices
items.content: arXiv:2611.22240v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Scenes captured with handheld and wearable cameras are still shipped to a CUDA workstation for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) training. Training on the device that captured them, or on its companion phone or laptop, requires more than translating kernels: GPUs and drivers differ in parallel features, memory limits, and command submission, and these differences decide whether a training schedule executes and returns the correct update. We present Cross3DGS, a cross-vendor, cross-platform Vulkan trainer that keeps one optimizer and chooses its execution schedule per device in two steps: rules on device limits, workload size, and observed driver failures exclude the schedules known not to run correctly, and a fixed preference order selects one of the remaining feasible schedules. The same core completes standard-quality training (30k updates, one million Gaussians) on every configuration we measured, spanning NVIDIA, Intel, Arm, Qualcomm, AMD, and Apple GPUs and including Android devices and an iPhone, whereas the existing portable trainers VkSplat and Brush do not run on some of the mobile GPUs. Averaged over 11 scenes on a workstation, Cross3DGS has higher quality than VkSplat with no significant difference in training time, and Brush reports about three times the training time at comparable quality. The final quality of Cross3DGS is nearly identical across devices. A mobile application turns a handheld capture into a viewable model entirely on the device.

items.title: PCRG: Training-Free Pruning and Caching of Reference Tokens for Video Generation
items.content: arXiv:2611.22717v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Reference-to-video diffusion transformers pack the variational autoencoder (VAE) latents of all references and the generated tokens into one full-attention sequence, in which reference tokens make up about half. Because attention cost grows quadratically with sequence length, these tokens take up an even larger share of the attention computation, yet most of them are static, smooth or irrelevant to the output. To accelerate reference-conditioned generation, we propose pruning and caching of reference tokens for video generation (PCRG), a training-free, plug-and-play method that uses two signals the model already computes to assign each reference token to one of three tiers, namely pruned, cached or kept. The first is a low-level redundancy r from VAE latents, since a token whose latent barely changes over time or across its neighbors adds little new content. The second is a high-level importance g from the vision-language-model (VLM) conditioner, where the attention that the prompt and any first or last frames pay to a token tells whether the output needs to read it. Tokens that are not redundant are kept, and redundant tokens are cached if important and pruned otherwise. Pruned tokens leave the sequence before the first step with all rotary position embedding positions unchanged. Cached tokens have their keys and values computed once and reused, and kept tokens are processed as usual. On MiniMax-H3, already distilled to 8 timesteps and quantized to int8, PCRG is 1.57x faster end to end on our V2V-Bench and 1.49x faster on the public VACE-Benchmark, while the quality of VBench drops by only 0.24% and 0.17%, respectively. PCRG shortens the sequence rather than changing how attention is computed or which steps are run, so it also stacks on step caching and sparse attention. On V2V-Bench it reaches 1.86x with TeaCache, 1.82x with Spark at nearly unchanged fidelity and 2.15x with Veda.

It is training-free and plug-and-play, using signals the model already computes to tier tokens into pruned, cached, or kept.

Efficiency gains for diffusion transformers are valuable, but the technique is an application of known KV/token-caching ideas to a specific architecture.

items.title: Wear and Go: Calibration Free Sparse Inertial Motion Capture via Online Sensor Setup Estimation
items.content: arXiv:2611.22894v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Sparse inertial motion capture typically assumes that each sensor's anatomical identity and mounting orientation are known. We present MOSAIC (Motion-based Sensor Assignment and Inertial Calibration), a framework that recovers this setup from ordinary motion without a calibration pose. Our central insight is that body pose changes continuously while the sensor setup persists, allowing movements that are individually ambiguous to provide complementary evidence over time. A setup network processes unordered sensor streams with temporal and cross-sensor attention, then accumulates assignment and rotation evidence into a session-level estimate. The recovered setup canonicalizes measurements for frozen pretrained pose estimators, separating sensor configuration from motion reconstruction. For sensors worn at prescribed body sites, evaluation on real inertial recordings with randomized setups shows near-calibrated pose accuracy for bounded offsets and substantial benefits from accumulation under arbitrary orientations. Transfer across pose networks supports setup recovery as a reusable interface between interchangeable sensors and pretrained pose models.
items.author: Yuanshuo Tan, Licheng Zhong
items.summary: MOSAIC removes the calibration-pose requirement in sparse inertial motion capture by recovering each sensor's anatomical assignment and mounting orientation from ordinary movement, exploiting that pose changes continuously while the sensor setup persists. A setup network with temporal and cross-sensor attention accumulates evidence into a session-level estimate that canonicalizes measurements for frozen pretrained pose estimators.
items.reasoning: The key insight (accumulating evidence over continuous motion to disambiguate sensor setup) is clean and the calibration-free property significantly improves usability of wearable motion capture. Separation of setup estimation from frozen pose estimators is architecturally neat, though the application area is specialized.

items.content_html: arXiv:2611.22894v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sparse inertial motion capture typically assumes that each sensor's anatomical identity and mounting orientation are known. We present MOSAIC (Motion-based Sensor Assignment and Inertial Calibration), a framework that recovers this setup from ordinary motion without a calibration pose. Our central insight is that body pose changes continuously while the sensor setup persists, allowing movements that are individually ambiguous to provide complementary evidence over time. A setup network processes unordered sensor streams with temporal and cross-sensor attention, then accumulates assignment and rotation evidence into a session-level estimate. The recovered setup canonicalizes measurements for frozen pretrained pose estimators, separating sensor configuration from motion reconstruction. For sensors worn at prescribed body sites, evaluation on real inertial recordings with randomized setups shows near-calibrated pose accuracy for bounded offsets and substantial benefits from accumulation under arbitrary orientations. Transfer across pose networks supports setup recovery as a reusable interface between interchangeable sensors and pretrained pose models.

items.title: Wall-to-wall maps of canopy height and aboveground carbon across the Atlantic Forest
items.content: arXiv:2611.23048v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Global canopy height maps are increasingly used to estimate forest carbon, yet their regional accuracy is rarely tested. We present wall-to-wall maps of canopy height (10~m) and aboveground carbon density (30~m) for the Brazilian Atlantic Forest in 2024. Height was predicted by a deep learning network fusing Sentinel-2 reflectance, Sentinel-1 and ALOS PALSAR backscatter and ALOS elevation, trained on 7{,}179 and tested on 1{,}793 patches (58{,}800~km$^2$) from a statewide airborne LiDAR campaign over S\~ao Paulo state, Brazil. On held-out test patches, the root mean square error is 3.05~m at 10~m and 2.58~m at 30~m, and the model was validated at two LiDAR sites outside S\~ao Paulo. Over the same pixels, the Meta and World Resources Institute global product has more than twice this error. A power law fitted to 124 inventory plots converted canopy height to above ground carbon density. The remaining forest holds 1{,}944~Tg~C over 28.3~Mha. Global products therefore need local validation before use in carbon accounting.

items.title: VLM-guided Grounding Expert for Generalised Referring Expression Comprehension
items.content: arXiv:2611.22625v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Generalised referring expression comprehension (GREC) aims to identify and localise the zero, one or multiple objects referred to by a language expression. In robotic manipulation, grounding also needs to remain accurate when requests for the same objects are paraphrased or embedded in additional context in robotics. However, grounding expert models are sensitive to instruction variation, while generative vision--language models (VLMs) struggle with complete target recovery and rejection of absent targets. These complementary limitations motivate combining the contextual representations of VLMs with the direct spatial prediction capabilities of grounding experts. We therefore introduce VLM-guided Grounding Expert (VGE), which combines a frozen VLM with a trainable grounding expert through layerwise joint attention and text-conditioned instance scoring. These interfaces leverage multimodal understanding of the VLM to guide object-query refinement and candidate selection while retaining direct bounding-box prediction. Across three datasets, VGE achieves the highest averaged F1 score among the evaluated methods on all five test splits, with differences of at most 1.2 percentage points across instruction conditions within each split. On the dataset with robotic scenes, VGE also achieves the highest F1 across instruction variants and no-target, single-target and multiple-target cases. VGE provides a $5.3$--$13.0\times$ inference speedup over the baseline with the same VLM base model. These results support combining VLM context with specialised spatial prediction to address both grounding challenges, with particularly strong performance in robotic scenes. Code will be released upon publication.
items.author: Mingcheng Zhu, Wentian Xu, Tao Lin, Shiying Duan, Ziyun Liang, Xuecheng Qi, Junyang Chen, Kuo Li, Zhifan Wan, Dong Wang, Richard Wang, Yang Gao
items.summary: VGE combines a frozen VLM's contextual representations with a grounding expert's direct spatial prediction to improve generalized referring expression comprehension, including rejection of absent targets and robustness to paraphrased, robot-contextualized requests. It targets reliable language grounding for robotic manipulation.
items.reasoning: Sensible and useful hybrid architecture addressing complementary weaknesses of VLMs and grounding experts, with direct robotics relevance; the combination strategy is somewhat incremental over existing fusion approaches.

items.title: [Research Note] Detecting Research Sabotage with Debate & Slopvestigators
items.content:
This work is ongoing as part of the SPAR program. The original proposal is here.

## TL;DR

In the coming years, we will likely rely increasingly on AIs to do alignment research on our behalf. In that world, it seems pretty crucial to be able to robustly check untrusted research for subtle sabotage, even when the research tasks are fuzzy and the automated researchers are extremely smart. This seems like a great use case for scalable oversight methods. To that end we directly tested the sabotage detection uplift from debate, and found little to no benefit from using a debate setup over a lone judge. However, we did see success with a decomposition strategy loosely inspired by both Extract-and-Evaluate and slopvestigation, where swarms of parallel agents investigate different potential well-scoped sabotages. This beat a lone judge by ~0.09 AUROC, though this remains within noise.

## Introduction

As AIs get smarter, and AI safety researchers rely more on AI, we run into the issue that our AIs might be subtly sabotaging our research. This poses a particular threat if our alignment plan depends on research done by superhuman AIs, where the outputs of such models are increasingly difficult to evaluate by humans or generated at a volume untenable for human review.

Auditing Sabotage Bench showed that humans perform quite poorly at identifying research sabotage! That is, when shown either (1) a real research codebase, or (2) a subtly sabotaged codebase, humans have a hard time differentiating the two. This seems like a perfect testbed for scalable oversight.

The central question is this: can we use debate protocols to improve LLM-judge performance on Auditing Sabotage Bench?

In this SPAR project we focused so far on:

- The potential performance lift gained from using debate protocols.
- How debate performs when an untrusted debater is actively sabotaging it.
- Whether there are other methods to uplift performance on ASB.

## Related Work...

items.title: DNeo: Your Parallel Draft Model Needs Better Target Feature Encoding
items.content: arXiv:2611.21925v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Speculative-diffusion decoding uses a small parallel drafter model to generate b draft tokens in one forward pass, which then undergo parallel verification via a larger target model. Faster inference can be achieved when multiple draft tokens pass verification simultaneously. Recent parallel draft architectures (DFlash, DSpark) improve draft quality by conditioning on rich features computed by the target, through a mechanism known as feature encoding. However, standard feature encoding mechanisms have three limitations: (1) they are lossy, applying encoding projections that are destructive to the underlying target feature-space via a discovered effect known as residual mixing, (2) they are memory-less, with no record of previously processed proposals, and (3) they utilize features sampled uniformly from across the target layers, omitting important hidden states. To address these issues, we propose Mixture-of-Features Attention (MoFA), a lightweight feature-encoding approach equipped with a working memory that encodes previously rejected proposals. Leveraging MoFA, rejection memory, and a set of further enhancements, including 2-tap causal convolutions, prefix-only cross-attention, and non-uniform target layer selection, the final architecture, DNeo, achieves 1.3x faster generation speed than SoTA (DFlash-2) without impacting drafter footprint or generation quality. DNeo marks a new state of the art in high quality, fast LLM inference.
items.author: Jameson Sandler, Shane Bergsma, Mostafa Elhoushi, Bin Claire Zhang, Gavia Gray, Joel Hestness, Nolan Dey, Ferdinando Fioretto
items.summary: DNeo improves speculative-diffusion decoding by fixing three limitations of feature-encoding mechanisms used by parallel drafters: lossy projections via residual mixing, lack of memory across steps, and related encoding inefficiencies. Better conditioning on target features should increase the fraction of draft tokens passing verification, speeding inference.
items.reasoning: A competent systems/efficiency contribution to an active inference-optimization area, with a clear identification of the residual-mixing effect and principled fixes. Impact is meaningful for practitioners but incremental relative to broader architectural advances, and gains depend on target-drafter pairings.

items.title: The Only Edge Was Memorized in Training: LLM Trading Agents Around Earnings and Bad News
items.content: arXiv:2611.22177v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Large language model (LLM) trading agents are tested on news, but news reaches stock prices within minutes, and a benchmark that replays headlines at their publication time finds no alpha in trading on them. Money can then remain in two places, before news whose date is known, such as earnings announcements, and after bad news, if the market's fall went too far. However, studies of LLMs and earnings read documents published with or after the announcement, and studies of reversal sort monthly portfolios, so neither tells whether an agent can trade these moments after costs. In this paper, we test LLM agents at both moments on the same look-ahead-free benchmark, before 598 earnings announcements and after 409 bad-news drops of large US stocks. Every input is cut at the decision close, staged agents are compared with single calls, simple rules and a logistic regression, and every decision is made with and without the stock's name. Across five models from four vendors, no agent beat the simple bets. Before earnings, the agents mostly bought and earned what buying before every announcement earned, and after bad news, a Gemini-based agent called almost every fall an overreaction while no agent picked better dips than buying them all. The only gains came from what the models had memorized in training. Given only the ticker and the dates, a GPT-based model called the direction of 59.2% of the announcements before its training cutoff and 53.3% after it. Agent builders should therefore compare an event agent with the simple bet and test it blind after the training cutoff.
items.author: Jackson Wang
items.summary: Using a look-ahead-free benchmark of 598 earnings announcements and 409 bad-news drops in large US stocks, the paper tests whether LLM trading agents can generate alpha after transaction costs at two exploitable moments: before scheduled news and after overreaction to bad news. The title suggests the only exploitable edge was memorized during training, a sobering result for LLM-based trading claims.
items.reasoning: A careful, look-ahead-free evaluation that usefully punctures hype around LLM trading agents with a single-author but methodologically cautious design; findings are finance-specific and negative-result in nature.

items.title: Think Once, Act Fast: Cost-Effective Recursive Self-Improvement for Decision Model Harness
items.content: arXiv:2611.22432v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Fast System-1 models enable responsive actions but struggle with complex or unfamiliar tasks. Large language model (LLM)-based System-2 provides strong reasoning capabilities, yet repeated invocation incurs substantial latency and computational costs. To bridge this gap, we propose JevRSI, a System-1/System-2 collaboration framework that transforms LLM reasoning into transferable decision support through recursive harness improvement. A Jev-style System-1 model enables low-latency action selection, while an asynchronous System-2 LLM develops a modular harness. The harness integrates procedures, state memory, and world models to provide decision contexts spanning the past, present, and future. Utility-driven retrieval selects modules based on both contextual relevance and their utility on previous tasks. Environmental feedback guides targeted revisions and enables recursive self-improvement. Experiments across three datasets show that JevRSI consistently improves decision quality, matching or surpassing LLM agents in several settings. It preserves low-latency execution with favorable performance-cost trade-offs. Moreover, System-2 development interventions decrease as the harness evolves, amortizing System-2 costs through continuous improvement. Our project is available at https://github.com/usail-hkust/JevRSI.
items.author: Siqi Lai, Haitao Li, Hao Liu
items.summary: JevRSI is a System-1/System-2 collaboration framework in which a fast, low-latency System-1 model handles action selection while an asynchronous LLM System-2 recursively builds a modular harness of procedures, state memory, and world models that supply decision context across past, present, and future. Utility-driven retrieval selects harness modules to cut the latency and compute costs of repeatedly invoking LLM reasoning.
items.reasoning: The cost-aware orchestration of slow reasoning into a reusable harness is a relevant direction given inference-cost pressures, and the recursive self-improvement framing is intriguing. However, the approach relies on several loosely specified components (harness, retrieval, world models), the venue and evaluation strength are unknown, and similar dual-system architectures have been explored before.

items.title: OICycle: Observe, Infer, and Intervene Cycle for Belief-State Learning in Longitudinal Clinical Decision Making
items.content: arXiv:2611.22826v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Clinical care is a closed loop: clinicians observe partial evidence, infer the patient's state, and intervene, and each intervention determines what is observed next. This makes clinical decision making a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP), in which a belief over a latent patient state must be updated from irregular, multimodal, and incomplete records. Yet most deep clinical models predict from a single snapshot or from coarsely aggregated history, while POMDP-based clinical methods need hand-specified discrete state spaces and transition models that real electronic health records cannot supply. We introduce OICycle (Observe, Infer, and Intervene Cycle), which learns a stochastic belief state directly from retrospective trajectories. At every episode, a learned recurrent operator fuses a sample of the previous belief with the new multimodal observations and the intervention that produced them. The resulting Gaussian belief is trained to predict clinicians' next interventions, the time to the next episode, and next-episode mortality. To enable reproducible evaluation, we release a benchmark derived from MIMIC-IV, MIMIC-IV-Note, and MIMIC-CXR that organizes 72,075 hospital admissions (5.4M laboratory, microbiology, radiology, prescription, and note records) into temporally ordered therapeutic--diagnostic episodes. Compared with an otherwise identical history-free model, OICycle improves next-intervention adaptive recall from 0.253 to 0.347, time-to-next-episode macro-F1 from 0.293 to 0.351, and next-episode mortality macro-F1 from 0.585 to 0.649. Analysis shows that the learned belief encodes intervention type and trajectory position and evolves smoothly across episodes, and that the benefit of history is concentrated in interventions whose ordering depends on prior findings.
items.author: Jitindra Fartiyal, Pedro Freire, Sergei K. Turitsyn, Sergei G. Solovski
items.summary: OICycle learns a stochastic belief state directly from retrospective electronic health records, framing longitudinal clinical decision making as a POMDP without requiring hand-specified discrete state spaces or transition models. It follows the observe-infer-intervene closed loop of clinical care, updating beliefs from irregular, multimodal, incomplete records. This bridges deep learning practicality with POMDP-style sequential decision making for medicine.
items.reasoning: A well-motivated combination of POMDP theory with deep learning on real EHR data, addressing a genuine gap where prior clinical POMDP methods need unrealistic hand-specified dynamics. Novelty is moderate — learned belief states exist in RL — but the clinical instantiation and data regime add value.

items.title: Improved Convergence Rates for Stochastic Multi-Gradient Descent which Close the Gap: A Proof by AI
items.content: arXiv:2607.18174v2 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: For smooth nonconvex stochastic multi-objective optimization, stochastic multi-gradient descent (SMG) computes an approximate steepest common descent direction of the objectives from stochastic gradients. Under standard assumptions, this note establishes a new convergence rate for SMG in terms of the squared Pareto-stationarity (PS) measure. With a constant stepsize and linearly growing mini-batches, the expected squared empirical PS measure at the algorithm's output is $\tilde{O}(T^{-1})$ after $T$ iterations. This improves on the $\tilde{O}(T^{-1/4})$ bound obtained by Chen et al. (JMLR, 2024) for linearly growing batches, without requiring bounded gradients. Here, $\tilde{O}(\cdot)$ suppresses logarithmic factors. The key to the rate improvement is to exploit the Lipschitz continuity of the PS measure, defined by the norm of the multi-gradient descent algorithm (MGDA) direction, rather than the $(1/2)$-H\"older continuity of the MGDA direction used by Chen et al. (2024). For variants of MoCo and MoCo+ with exact MGDA updates and constant batch sizes, the analysis gives expected squared empirical PS rates of $O(T^{-1/2})$ and $\tilde{O}(T^{-2/3})$, respectively. These bounds match the corresponding single-objective momentum rates up to logarithmic factors. The proof was accidentally discovered while the author was preparing homework for a graduate course: ChatGPT 5.4 Thinking Extended generated the initial proof strategy for the main SMG result in response to an author-written homework-solution prompt; the author then verified and reorganized the resulting argument. The appendices document the prompt, summarize the student submissions with LLM disclosures, and present additional proofs and results on momentum-based stochastic MGDA.
items.author: Lisha Chen
items.summary: This note establishes a new convergence rate for stochastic multi-gradient descent in smooth nonconvex multi-objective optimization, improving the squared Pareto-stationarity bound from O(T^-1/4) to O(T^-1) with constant stepsize and linearly growing mini-batches, without bounded-gradient assumptions. Notably, the key step in the proof was produced with AI assistance, as the title highlights. The result closes a gap in the multi-objective optimization literature.

However, it is a focused note on a specific algorithm rather than a broad advance, and multi-gradient methods are a specialized corner of optimization.

items.content_html: arXiv:2607.18174v2 Announce Type: cross Abstract: For smooth nonconvex stochastic multi-objective optimization, stochastic multi-gradient descent (SMG) computes an approximate steepest common descent direction of the objectives from stochastic gradients. Under standard assumptions, this note establishes a new convergence rate for SMG in terms of the squared Pareto-stationarity (PS) measure. With a constant stepsize and linearly growing mini-batches, the expected squared empirical PS measure at the algorithm's output is $\tilde{O}(T^{-1})$ after $T$ iterations. This improves on the $\tilde{O}(T^{-1/4})$ bound obtained by Chen et al. (JMLR, 2024) for linearly growing batches, without requiring bounded gradients. Here, $\tilde{O}(\cdot)$ suppresses logarithmic factors. The key to the rate improvement is to exploit the Lipschitz continuity of the PS measure, defined by the norm of the multi-gradient descent algorithm (MGDA) direction, rather than the $(1/2)$-H\"older continuity of the MGDA direction used by Chen et al. (2024). For variants of MoCo and MoCo+ with exact MGDA updates and constant batch sizes, the analysis gives expected squared empirical PS rates of $O(T^{-1/2})$ and $\tilde{O}(T^{-2/3})$, respectively. These bounds match the corresponding single-objective momentum rates up to logarithmic factors. The proof was accidentally discovered while the author was preparing homework for a graduate course: ChatGPT 5.4 Thinking Extended generated the initial proof strategy for the main SMG result in response to an author-written homework-solution prompt; the author then verified and reorganized the resulting argument. The appendices document the prompt, summarize the student submissions with LLM disclosures, and present additional proofs and results on momentum-based stochastic MGDA.

items.title: ARC-2: Continuous Compliance Through Delta Management
items.content: arXiv:2611.21811v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: ARC 1 introduced a three-layer governance architecture for autonomous systems comprising model safety validation, cognitive certification (CRAB), and operational authorization (LEA). However, it did not address how compliance should be maintained after deployment.   This paper introduces Delta Management, a continuous governance framework that measures deviations between a system's current operational state and its certified baseline, defined as a region rather than a fixed point. Compliance is assessed through continuous monitoring instead of static certification.   Four extensions are proposed. First, CRAB evaluation incorporates the worst verified behavioral deviations, with isolated outliers quarantined pending confirmation to prevent unjustified restrictions. Second, a layered trigger taxonomy distinguishes hard safety violations, critical single-dimension failures, correlated multi-system degradation, and risk-weighted composite indicators, each triggering proportionate responses. Third, a graduated safe transition protocol separates withdrawal of operational authorization from physical shutdown, consistent with established safety standards and EU AI Act requirements. Fourth, environmental delta is introduced as a distinct baseline validity condition: environmental drift beyond the certified Operational Design Domain (ODD) triggers recertification or ODD revision rather than automatic authority contraction.   Together, these extensions transform ARC from a deployment-time certification architecture into a continuous framework for monitoring, evaluating, and enforcing compliance throughout the operational lifecycle of autonomous systems. The framework addresses the continuous compliance obligations established by EU AI Act Article 72(2).

items.title: GauntletScore: Auditable Fact-Checking That Matches the Best Published Checkers on LLM-AggreFact
items.content: arXiv:2611.22027v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Checking whether a generated sentence is supported by its source document is a standard safeguard for AI-written text, and the strongest published checkers are single models. We describe GauntletScore, an evidence engine whose few rules and thresholds were set on the benchmark's development split. It puts typed questions to independent readers from different providers and records each answer as a measurement in an evidence ledger. It combines the measurements with a fixed Bayesian rule that counts a contradiction only when two readers agree. On the full LLM-AggreFact test split (29,320 claims across 11 datasets), following the leaderboard's approach, GauntletScore achieves 79.51 balanced accuracy, above every average published on the leaderboard as of 15 November 2026. That places it level with the best of them, nimble-v4-max (79.45 from its published dataset scores; the engine's 95% interval, 78.47 to 80.53, contains it). On the same claims it beats two of its three readers used alone (Readers A and B) by 1.66 and 2.17 points (95% intervals 0.80 to 2.53 and 1.29 to 3.06). Without AggreFact-CNN, described below, the leads are 0.90 and 1.32 and both intervals stay above zero. The engine also records the evidence behind every verdict, which a single model does not. Its largest margin is on full-length news articles checked against multi-sentence summaries (AggreFact-CNN), a format that resembles much regulated writing. There it scores 76.45, the best on the leaderboard, against 70.1 for the next best and 63.9 to 67.8 for the six systems with the highest averages. The test split was run once, on an engine frozen before the first test claim, under a stopping plan committed in advance. We release per-claim predictions and the scoring script.

items.title: Solver-Free and Cost-Aware Online Scheduling of AI Data Center Tasks
items.content: arXiv:2611.22239v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: AI data centers receive computing tasks continuously, whereas solver-based optimization takes time to run and electricity is priced per settlement period. This paper bridges this timing gap through a solver-free online optimization rule inspired by dual decomposition. The rule assigns each task a start period upon arrival to optimize energy cost subject to operational constraints, shifting flexible tasks toward low-price periods while keeping high-priority tasks on schedule. Simulations on the A100 GPU trace (3,456 GPUs, 1,343 tasks) show that the proposed rule keeps GPU and CPU use within capacity while scheduling tasks at low cost. Compared with a multi-timescale optimization benchmark, it achieves a lower cost and, because it needs no solver, much less computation time.
items.author: Xin Qin, Dawei Qiu, Fei Teng

items.title: Deal With It: On Better Schedules for Listwise Reranking
items.content: arXiv:2611.22392v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Listwise LLM rerankers cannot reliably rank hundreds of documents in a single call, and rely on schedules to orchestrate their calls. Parallel schedules split candidates into groups and advance a fixed quota from each. When a group holds more of the top passages than its quota, some are cut, and expensive repair calls become required. We show that the way candidates are split matters where such a quota can bind, and that, in expected cuts, the best split there deals them round-robin by retriever rank, like cards. Although not conceptually new, dealing has remained unanalyzed. We prove that, under a simple retriever model, no split with equal quotas cuts fewer of the true top ten on average, and that contiguous chunks cut more as the retriever improves. DealRank, the simplest schedule our analysis allows, is on average within 0.1 nDCG@10 points of the best schedules over six LLMs, in two rounds. It is consistently 1.1 to 1.4 times faster than BlitzRank with concurrent first calls up to a thousand candidates. There, it needs three rounds and is eleven times faster than the sliding window. In existing schedules such as BlitzRank, dealing reduces repair calls from 59% of queries to 14%, improving latency with no significant change in quality. Random partitioning appears equivalent at a quota of four, as predicted, but ties results to the seed and trails by 1.3 nDCG@10 points at a quota of one over a dense retriever.

Although dealing is not conceptually new, this is its first formal analysis for reranking schedules.
