items.content_html: arXiv:2611.23155v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Recent advances in text-to-image generation have substantially improved image quality, particularly through diffusion-based methods that require multiple inference steps. In contrast, Sphere Encoder offers an efficient generative framework capable of producing images with fewer forward steps. However, extending it to free-form text is nontrivial, because its class-conditioned design lacks cross-modal alignment. To address this challenge, we propose TextSphere, an efficient text-to-image generative framework that extends Sphere Encoder with language conditioning and cross-modal alignment. We incorporate pretrained CLIP text embeddings through adaptive layer normalization (AdaLN) to guide image generation while retaining the original spherical sampling mechanism. To bridge the cross-modal representation gap, we introduce a Spherical Semantic Alignment and Uniformity (SSAU) objective that jointly promotes semantic alignment and representation uniformity on the hypersphere. Experiments on CUB-200-2011, MS-COCO-2014, and Flickr30k demonstrate that TextSphere consistently reduces generation FID (gFID) over the text-conditioned baseline while achieving reconstruction FID (rFID) below 1.0. With only 4 and 6 sampling steps, TextSphere achieves lower gFID than the compared diffusion- and GAN-based models trained from scratch on CUB-200-2011 and MS-COCO-2014, respectively. We further observe that improved reconstruction fidelity does not necessarily yield better generation quality. In addition, we use Partial Least Squares Singular Value Decomposition (PLS-SVD) to analyze cross-modal alignment and modality gap, offering insight into the effectiveness of our approach.

items.title: Joint-ID: Transformer-based Joint Image Enhancement and Depth Estimation for Underwater Environments
items.content: arXiv:2611.22212v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Underwater imaging is a challenging task due to factors such as scattering, absorption, and turbulence, which degrade image quality and limit visibility. In this paper, we propose a novel approach for enhancing underwater images that leverages the benefits of joint learning for simultaneous image enhancement and depth estimation. We introduce Joint-ID, a transformer-based neural network that can obtain high-perceptual image quality and depth information from raw underwater images. Our approach formulates a multi-modal objective function that addresses invalid depth, lack of sharpness, and image degradation based on color and local texture. We design an end-to-end training pipeline that enables joint restoration and depth estimation in a shared hierarchical feature space. Additionally, we propose a synthetic dataset with various distortions and scene depths for multi-task learning. We evaluate Joint-ID on synthetic and standard datasets, as well as real underwater images with diverse spectra and harsh turbidity, demonstrating its effectiveness for underwater image enhancement and depth estimation. Furthermore, we demonstrate the ability of Joint-ID to perform feature matching and saliency detection for visually guided underwater robots. Our proposed method has the potential to improve the visual perception of underwater environments and benefit applications such as oceanography and underwater robotics. Supplements are available at: https://sites.google.com/view/joint-id/home

items.title: Reliability-Driven Feature Correction for Hyperspectral and LiDAR Classification
items.content: arXiv:2611.22508v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Hyperspectral image (HSI) and LiDAR data provide complementary spectral and elevation information for land-cover classification. However, the spatially varying class-discriminative reliability of modality features is rarely modeled explicitly, allowing weak or ambiguous features to adversely affect cross-modal interaction and fusion. To address this issue, we propose ReDF, a reliability-driven framework that quantifies the reliability of each modality's features at each spatial location through the strength of class-related evidence they provide, and uses it to guide feature correction and fusion. Specifically, a Reliability-Guided Feature Correction module introduces a class prototype bank for each modality and converts feature-prototype similarities into class evidence for reliability estimation. The estimated reliabilities are used to construct a reliability-weighted shared representation and to guide bidirectional cross-modal feature correction based on neighborhood agreement, refining modality features with weak class evidence through information from the other modality. Building on these outputs, a Reliability-Guided Feature Reweighting module conditions a low-rank modulation on the estimated reliabilities and the cross-modal disagreement, and applies it to the corrected modality-specific descriptors to adaptively rescale each modality's contribution to the fused representation used for final classification. Experiments on three public HSI-LiDAR datasets show higher mean overall accuracy and Kappa than the compared methods.

items.title: LUTBench: Benchmarking Text-Driven Photographic Look Transfer
items.content: arXiv:2611.23113v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Photographic color grading shapes the tone and color of a photograph to achieve a desired look. Text-driven photographic look transfer lets users specify these adjustments in natural language, with the goal of reproducing the requested look across photographs while preserving their content. However, prior research on text-driven color grading uses different datasets, text instructions, target definitions, and metrics. These differences make it difficult to compare how faithfully the methods reproduce the same look. To compare methods under a shared protocol, we introduce LUTBench. We collect 91 three-dimensional lookup tables (3D LUTs) and define one photographic look per LUT with a specified input conversion. Applying these looks to 5,000 MIT-Adobe FiveK photographs produces 455,000 input-target image pairs with reproducible target images. For each look, we use templates to turn measured tone and color changes on fixed color samples into candidate clauses. We use training image measurements to verify applicable clauses before composing the text description. The evaluation measures target fidelity, tests sensitivity to predefined input conversions, and separates generalization to unseen looks from reproduction of seen looks on new photographs. Across 16 methods, stronger text alignment does not guarantee target fidelity. However, most supervised variants improve fidelity on both seen and unseen looks.

items.title: Fully Spiking Neural Implementation of Lambda-Calculus Beta-Reduction via Biologically Documented Mechanisms
items.content: arXiv:2611.23182v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: We present the first complete implementation of $\beta$-reduction in the untyped $\lambda$-calculus using exclusively spiking neural dynamics. Every step of the reduction---redex detection, subterm segmentation, variable-binding detection, De~Bruijn index arithmetic, token copying, and inter-step role maintenance---is performed by leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neurons with explicit membrane dynamics, exponential synaptic currents, axonal delays, and pair-based spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP). Each neural component maps onto a specific, experimentally documented mechanism: Jeffress-type delay-line coincidence for redex detection; a line-attractor balance counter for subterm segmentation; $\theta$--$\gamma$ cross-frequency coupling for De~Bruijn variable binding; a phase-ring traveling wave for depth-index arithmetic; theta-cycle STDP for token copying; and recurrent persistent firing for role maintenance between reduction steps. All synaptic weights are derived analytically from measured EPSP amplitudes; no hand tuning is performed. The closed-loop system achieves 100\,\% agreement with a symbolic oracle across ten validation classes, including Church numeral arithmetic (\textsc{plus}, \textsc{mult}, \textsc{pred}), Boolean logic with divergent branches, Y-combinator steps, terms with up to six bound-variable occurrences, De~Bruijn indices up to~12, noise robustness, and determinism. To our knowledge this is the first Turing-complete symbolic computation performed entirely within spike dynamics using biologically grounded circuit primitives. We discuss implications for neuromorphic proof assistants and the neural basis of symbolic reasoning.

items.title: Arboreus: A Realistic Boreal Forest Simulator with Topographic Terrain and Satellite-Informed Parametric Tree Distributions
items.content: arXiv:2611.22908v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: This work presents Arboreus, a realistic Boreal forest simulator, developed to support statistical validation of robotic autonomy algorithms in Boreal forest environments. Arboreus presents an automated methodology for synthesizing large-scale, data-informed, plausible forest worlds from parametric trees, height-variant terrain, and satellite-informed tree density distributions. The parametric generation of dominant Boreal tree species such as Birch, Spruce, and Pine is guided by trunk, canopy, and foliage parameters, extracted from growth studies in the Nordic areas. Tree distribution in an area of interest is guided by the Copernicus satellite dataset, which provides tree cover density and dominant species type at up to 10m raster resolution. The forest floor generation is guided by topographic data from the Swedish cadastral agency to produce realistic data-informed terrains. Given coordinates and extents of forested areas of interest, Arboreus synthesizes data-informed plausible forests, while offering flexibility to inject user observations of real forests (detail, age, dimensionality and tree count), which is critical for realistic synthetic data generation and for the testing of feature-sensitive autonomy algorithms. The applicability of Arboreus for benchmarking and validation of robot autonomy for different robot mobilities is demonstrated in Gazebosim, Unreal Engine, and Isaac Sim physics engines. The applicability of Arboreus as a source of synthetic forest data and its potential to support downstream forest resource mapping research (volume estimation, tree instance segmentation and stem attribute estimation) is also demonstrated. Arboreus has been open-sourced along with a dataset comprising 25 Boreal forest worlds of size 1000m2 corresponding to three real forest sites.

items.title: Locally Linear Generalized Single Index Regression
items.content: arXiv:2611.22011v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: In this work we propose and analyze a procedure for estimating a generalized single-index regression model. This generalized single-index regression framework models the conditional mean of the responses $Y$ as a function of the covariates $X$ where the mapping is assumed to have the form $f \circ g$, where $g$ is $\beta$-H\"older with $\beta \geq 2$ and $f$ can be a discontinuous function of bounded variation. We propose a general procedure that operates under minimal assumptions about the distribution of covariates $X$, requiring only boundedness, sufficient smoothness and absolute continuity with respect to Lebesgue. Our procedure jointly estimates the gradient vector $\hat v(x) \approx \nabla g(x)$ and the conditional mean $\mu(x) = f(g(x))$ by solving a localized weighted linear least squares problem. We derive central limit theorems for gradient vector estimates $\hat{v}_x$ and regression estimates $\hat{\mu}(x)$, and we derive rates of convergence for our approach, illustrating that it indeed achieves a stochastic convergence rate matching the minimax mean squared error rate when $\beta = 2$ and $f$ has a locally Lipschitz derivative. Unlike prior approaches our velocity estimation results accommodate link functions in the local bounded-variation class, allowing for nonsmooth and even discontinuous links while retaining consistency and asymptotic normality at almost every inference point. Finally, we instantiate this model in the situation where $g = \Pi$ is a closest point projection onto a compact and regular embedded $C^3$ curve $\gamma$, a setting recently studied in the literature. We also supplement our theoretical results with experiments on real and synthetic data to demonstrate the utility of our procedure.

items.title: The case against smoking (decision theory)
items.content:
I here make the case against smoking in the Smoking Lesion, a hypothetical decision scenario (where smoking doesn't cause cancer) studied in decision theory. For the case against smoking in real life (where smoking does cause cancer), see, for example, the Wikipedia article on the health effects of tobacco or the Cleveland Clinic article about smoking.

I assume basic familiarity with the debate about Newcomb’s problem and the basic mechanisms of evidential and causal decision theory (EDT and CDT). I assume some sympathy with one-boxing.

The Smoking Lesion goes as follows:

Some people have a genetic lesion that causes cancer and also makes them more likely to smoke. As a result, smokers get cancer much more often than non-smokers. Unlike in the real world, smoking itself doesn't cause cancer. You don't know whether you have the lesion. You enjoy smoking, but cancer is much worse than smoking is pleasant. Should you smoke?

People usually use the Smoking Lesion to argue against EDT. In particular, they claim that EDT reasons as follows: Smoking is evidence that you have the lesion. So conditional on smoking, you're more likely to get cancer than conditional on not smoking. Since cancer is much worse than smoking is pleasant, you shouldn't smoke.

People typically take this reasoning to be mistaken. They then conclude that EDT is wrong and turn to some other kind of decision theory that doesn’t use conditionals in the way that EDT does. (Some people still try to get their new theory to one-box. Examples of such theories are timeless decision theory (TDT), functional decision theory (FDT), and Spohn's version of CDT (Spohn 2012). Others take the Smoking Lesion to be a reductio ad absurdum of one-boxing and thus end up endorsing a theory like CDT that two-boxes.)...
items.author: Caspar Oesterheld
items.summary: Caspar Oesterheld argues that evidential decision theory can recommend against smoking in the Smoking Lesion thought experiment, contrary to the standard use of that scenario as a counterexample to EDT. Assuming familiarity with Newcomb's problem and one-boxing intuitions, the post builds a technical case within formal decision theory.
items.reasoning: A rigorous conceptual contribution from a respected decision-theory researcher in the alignment community, challenging a canonical counterexample. It matters for decision-theory foundations relevant to alignment, but it is a niche theoretical argument with no direct empirical or applied impact.

items.title: TRIDENT: Efficient Triple-Task Learning of Dehazing, Depth, and Uncertainty Estimation for Underwater 3-D Robot Visual Perception
items.content: arXiv:2611.22224v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Underwater visual systems often suffer from blurry textures and low color contrast due to the inevitable light propagation. These issues can significantly degrade the perception of stable robotic operations. In this paper, we introduce a novel learning-based sensing system that tackles the multidimensional vision tasks in underwater; concretely, we deal with image enhancement, depth estimation, and uncertainty for 3-D visual systems. Also, we propose a TRIDENT model in a fast and lightweight manner; TRIDENT consists of three parallelized decoders and one backbone structure for efficient feature sharing. In addition, it is designed to be trained to express complex parameterization. In experimental evaluation on several standard datasets, we demonstrate that TRIDENT significantly outperforms other existing methods on image enhancement and depth estimation. Despite performing three tasks, our model has better efficiency than the others for both memory size and inference time. Finally, our joint learning approach demonstrates robustness in feature matching and seamlessly extends from 2-D to 3-D vision tasks. Supplements are available at https://sites.google.com/view/underwater-trident/home

items.title: Plenty to FRET About: From Hazard Analysis to Formal Requirements for Robot-Assisted Dressing
items.content: arXiv:2611.22399v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Understanding requirements for systems involving humans and robots is essential for providing robust evidence that such systems behave correctly. Requirements formalisation approaches such as the Formal Requirements Elicitation Tool (FRET) can support the transition from unstructured natural language to formal representations suitable for verification. In this paper, we formalise 146 hazard-derived natural-language requirements for a Robot-Assisted Dressing (RAD) case study, previously classified using a taxonomy of Human-Robot Teamwork (HRT) requirements. Through an iterative process involving domain-expert clarification, these were represented by 117 unique FRETISH requirements. Formalisation exposed ambiguities, temporal and probabilistic assumptions, and cases where source requirements needed to be decomposed or could be consolidated because they expressed the same formal behaviour. Temporal analysis showed that 70.1% of the unique FRETISH requirements use either immediate-response or ordering constraints (immediately or before), while formalisation also exposed relationships between requirements across HRT taxonomy categories. We further analyse the formal semantics and realisability of the resulting requirements. The results show that HRT classification and formalisation provide complementary views: the taxonomy captures the teamwork concern represented by a requirement, while FRETISH makes the required behaviour explicit. We report practical lessons and limitations of applying FRET to HRT requirements and identify directions for further work.
items.author: Gunjari Chakraborty (University of Manchester), Yasmin Rafiq (University of Manchester), Hazel M. Taylor (University of Manchester), Marie Farrell (University of Manchester)

items.title: Can Activation Steering Substitute for Prompt-Based Affective Priming in LLM Digital Twins?
items.content: arXiv:2611.22738v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Affective priming -- asking participants to write about a recalled event, such as a time they felt grateful or lacked control, and then measuring the induced state and its spillover onto related judgments -- is a standard way to manipulate emotion in the social sciences, and it also shifts the responses of LLM-based digital twins. The writing task, however, requires generating a full text. We test whether activation steering can replace it. Using Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on 100 personas in two domains (gratitude, lack of control), we compare a real-prompt path replicating the original Twin-2K-500 Mega Study (J2) with an injection path that skips the writing and adds a mean-difference direction, extracted from human writing, to the residual stream at varying strengths. The real-prompt effects fall between the original human and digital-twin effects in 5 of 6 comparisons. Injection shifts the manipulation check in a dose-dependent way and matches the real-prompt effect at one strength in the gratitude domain (beta ~ 2.7), but overshoots beyond it, on the proximal measure as well, and asymmetrically across the two directions. A structure-matched No-Injection baseline separates two sources of difference: omitting the writing task raises the proximal measure in both domains, whereas the injected direction itself moves a distal measure in the lack-of-control domain. Substitution is therefore measure-dependent: validity established for one way of inducing a state does not carry over uniformly to another.

The question matters for efficient simulation of human-subject experiments.

items.title: RLDE: A Reinforcement Learning Framework for Interpretable Iterative Document Editing
items.content: arXiv:2611.22039v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Improving the quality, clarity, and flow of long documents remains a challenging problem in NLP, as human editing typically occurs through iterative refinement rather than a single-pass rewrite. Most existing automated systems act as black-box generators or rely on supervised learning, limiting interpretability and failing to capture the sequential nature of revisions. In this paper, we propose RLDE, an automated end-to-end metric-driven RL framework that formulates document revision as a reference-free MDP problem (unsupervised with respect to paired document-revision targets). Working with a limited action space (NOOP, INSERT, DELETE, REPLACE), RLDE leverages Pointer Networks for dynamic span selection at the token level and sends generative actions to the frozen BART-base model to obtain context-aware suggestions. PPO agents learn to optimize a multi-objective reward function based on readability, perplexity, and grammar metrics with the help of a novel SBERT-based Semantic Preservation Penalty constraint to avoid deletion degeneracy. Evaluations on the BEA-2019 dataset showed statistically significant results (p < 0.01) across all metrics, where Flesch Reading Ease increased from 49.8 to 59.4, perplexity decreased from 63.7 to 39.8, while preserving 93% of semantic information. When compared to Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompt-engineered models like GPT-4 and LLaMA-2, RLDE shows high performance at a very low computational inference cost. Moreover, the quality of edits generated by RLDE has been verified via human evaluations, scoring 4.9/5 for meaning preservation and 4.4/5 for edit quality.
items.author: Nikhil Parkar, M. Marimuthu, Riya Joshi, Karthikeyan N
items.summary: RLDE formulates long-document revision as a reference-free MDP with a small action space (NOOP, INSERT, DELETE, REPLACE), using Pointer Networks for token-level span selection and a metric-driven reward to mimic iterative human editing rather than one-pass rewriting. The authors frame it as more interpretable than black-box generators and trainable without paired revision data.
items.reasoning: The iterative, interpretable framing of document editing is sensible, but the reliance on a metric-driven reward invites Goodhart-style optimization, and Pointer-Network-based edit systems predate modern LLM editors. The abstract does not indicate strong empirical dominance over simpler LLM-based revision approaches.

items.title: SLED: Sensor SLicing from Edge to Datacenter
items.content: arXiv:2611.21937v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Modern sensing systems generate large volumes of heterogeneous data streams from multiple sensor modalities, increasing reliance on datacenters for computation, artificial intelligence/superintelligence (AI/SI) inference, and AI/SI training. Each sensor stream may have different network and compute requirements depending on its type and data volume. However, current wireless systems typically allocate resources at the device level, leading to contention among co-located sensor streams, where bulk data transfers may starve latency-critical telemetry. To this end, this paper introduces Sensor Slicing (SL). SL provides deterministic, medium access control (MAC)-level isolation for individual sensors within a single user equipment (UE) in open radio access networks (O-RAN). Using agentic coding techniques, SL is implemented in two O-RAN-compliant packages, reducing development time by 400 times (2 h 40 min [OCUDU] vs. 6.5 weeks [OAI]), 228-fold fewer human prompts (4 vs. 913), and less than half the tokens (0.64B vs. 1.43B). An associated end-to-end framework, SLED, is implemented to establish per-sensor radio and network isolation across edge, campus, and remote high-performance computing (HPC) tiers. Over-the-air wireless experiments demonstrate that while conventional network slicing causes critical delays to increase more than 2,300-fold under high traffic load, SLED maintains stable latency. Scaling evaluations on the two RAN stacks show that throughput remains within 0.9% and 1.4% of expected allocations even as the number of sensor slices increases. The results demonstrate that SLED preserves latency-critical telemetry while effectively utilizing resources across the sensor-to-HPC pipeline. The SLED software and evaluation datasets are publicly available at https://github.com/UNL-CPN-Lab/SLED-Sensor-SLicing-from-Edge-to-Datacenter.
items.author: Alan Subedi, Avhishek Biswas, Apala Pramanik, Amlan Balabantaray, Mikhail Titov, Santosh Pitla, Ozgur Kilic, Mehmet C. Vuran

items.title: Measuring Human-AI Alignment as an Early Indicator for Effective Collaboration in Hybrid SE Teams
items.content: arXiv:2611.21633v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: As AI agents increasingly integrate into software engineering (SE) processes, ensuring effective collaboration in these hybrid teams becomes a critical challenge. While existing metrics focus on observing dynamic run-time performance, there is a lack of systematic, static measurements for early human-AI alignment -- the degree to which an AI's actions and granularity map to human expectations. This position paper proposes a research agenda to develop an SE-specific alignment metric suite drawing principles from software architecture, organizational psychology, and human-computer interaction. Furthermore, it outlines a validation methodology using concepts and techniques from business process monitoring (BPM) and introduces static assessment tools leveraging declarative BPM languages to ensure agents adhere to specific project constraints.
items.author: Andreas Metzger
items.summary: This position paper proposes a research agenda for measuring static, early-stage human-AI alignment in hybrid software engineering teams — how well an AI's actions and granularity match human expectations — going beyond run-time performance metrics. It outlines an SE-specific alignment metric suite drawing on software architecture, organizational psychology, and HCI, with a validation methodology borrowed from business process monitoring. As a position paper, it frames an agenda rather than presenting empirical results.
items.reasoning: A reasonable framing of an under-measured concept (static human-AI alignment in SE teams) with a concrete validation plan, but it is a position paper with no empirical results. Interdisciplinary framing is sensible; impact depends entirely on follow-through by the community.

items.title: Segmentation-Guided Direct Capacity Estimation of Rooftop Photovoltaics from Aerial Imagery
items.content: arXiv:2611.22076v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Distribution planners need installation-level inventories of rooftop photovoltaic (PV) capacity, but interconnection records may be incomplete or spatially aggregated. Conventional image-based estimators segment PV arrays, convert the mask to physical area, and multiply by an estimated power density, coupling capacity prediction to mask-derived area. We propose Direct Head, a segmentation-guided architecture that retains U-Net segmentation and soft-mask pooling while directly regressing nonnegative capacity from PV-region features and area descriptors. We evaluate three independent runs on 7,590 French rooftop installations under the original split and a department-based holdout. Relative to a parameter-matched area-density neural model, Direct Head reduces mean absolute error by 8.7% and 12.5%, and symmetric mean absolute percentage error by 14.0% and 20.7%, respectively. Comparisons with conventional estimators, controlled architecture variants, auxiliary-loss ablations, and representative cases show that segmentation provides useful spatial evidence without requiring capacity to be determined by an area-density product.
items.author: Guibin Chen, Emma Fan, Yuzhang Lin
items.summary: The paper proposes Direct Head, an architecture that keeps U-Net segmentation and soft-mask pooling but directly regresses nonnegative rooftop PV capacity from region features and area descriptors, decoupling prediction from mask-derived area times power density. Evaluated on 7,590 French rooftop installations across three runs and a department-based holdout, it improves on a parameter-matched area-density model.
items.reasoning: A competent applied computer-vision contribution with real value for grid planning, using a sensible architectural fix to a known estimation-pipeline fragility. Novelty is incremental and the evaluation is regional (French data), which somewhat limits generalization claims.

items.title: Anticipating or Speculating? Making Futures Pay in AI Ethics
items.content: arXiv:2611.22268v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Philosophers have recently been trying to develop uniform decision rules for instances in which physicians' judgments diverge from the recommendations of medical artificial intelligence (AI) systems. I argue that this effort is fatally flawed because the performance and appropriate use of algorithmic recommendation systems by physicians are highly context-specific, empirical medical matters rather than epistemological ones. In such instances, general decision rules can be stipulated only to the extent that they abstract away from relevant, indeed determinative, contextual circumstances. The alleged problem of physician-AI disagreement, and others like it, play into longstanding disputes in technology ethics about the viability and utility of envisioning possible futures: is this useful "anticipation" or wasteful "speculation"? I suggest that the two may be distinguished. Anticipation explores plausible futures to help inform present actions under irreducible uncertainty. Speculation abstracts away uncertainty, developing formal solutions to stipulated circumstances whose relationship to the real present is often quite unclear. Efforts to develop crisp philosophical solutions to physician-AI disagreement, among other problems, fall into the latter category. Technology ethics should remember that fruitful futures thinking must both begin from and return to the messy, uncertain present.
items.author: John P. Nelson
items.summary: This philosophy paper argues that attempts to build uniform decision rules for physician-AI disagreement in medical settings are fatally flawed because algorithmic recommendation use is context-specific and empirical rather than epistemological. The author contends general rules abstract away determinative contextual circumstances.
items.reasoning: A well-argued philosophical critique relevant to AI-assisted decision-making governance, but it is a conceptual argument without empirical content and its practical influence on the field is uncertain.

items.title: Hierarchical Control of Antiphase Synchronization in Biomorphic Spiking Neural Architectures for Locomotor Control
items.content: arXiv:2611.22639v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Central pattern generators (CPGs) provide a biologically inspired foundation for adaptive locomotor control, yet systematically characterizing their dynamic regimes in spiking neural networks remains challenging. This study introduces a framework for identifying and stabilizing antiphase synchronization in a biomorphic spiking CPG model embedded in a closed neuromuscular loop. A composite synchronization metric is developed, integrating phase coherence, amplitude balance, and temporal stability. Its performance is evaluated across systematically varied stimulation waveforms and synaptic configurations. Statistical analysis reveals that stimulation type dominates regime determination, with tonic drive yielding the most robust antiphase synchronization. Periodic inputs induce nonlinear saturation and context-dependent network routing. Although synaptic weights alone show limited discriminative power, they significantly modulate robustness within a given stimulation context, with reciprocal Ia interneuron connections emerging as key stabilizers. The proposed composite metric achieves robust antiphase detection, outperforming traditional phase-only measures while preserving biophysical interpretability. These findings establish a statistically validated, hierarchical modeling approach in which external drive defines the operating regime and targeted synaptic configurations fine-tune dynamic stability, providing actionable guidelines for closed-loop neuromechanical controllers and adaptive neuroprosthetic interfaces.

This informs biologically inspired locomotor control with spiking networks.

items.title: Fine-Tuning Gemma 4 Edge Models for MATLAB Signal-Processing Code with SFT and QLoRA on a Laptop iGPU
items.content: arXiv:2611.23205v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Small language models that run on a laptop are attractive for writing signal-processing code offline, but they make systematic errors on digital signal processing (DSP) conventions. We apply supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to the Gemma 4 edge models E2B and E4B with 66 checked examples covering 11 signal-processing MATLAB subtasks, using low-rank adaptation (LoRA) and quantized LoRA (QLoRA) on the integrated GPU (iGPU) of a laptop, and deploy the 8-bit integer (int8) models with the adapters through OpenVINO. On held-out variants scored by deterministic checkers, the pass rate rises from 18/66 to 37/66 (LoRA) and 37/66 (QLoRA) for E2B and from 32/66 to 47/66 for E4B (QLoRA). Reading all 159 failing programs shows that the adapters remove most errors of convention, such as the sign of a lag, units and array shapes, but few errors in building signals and noise. Applied at run time, the adapter costs 17-19% of the generation speed.
items.author: Mehmet Altan Toks\"oz
items.summary: This applied paper fine-tunes Gemma 4 edge models (E2B and E4B, existing since April 2026) with SFT, LoRA, and QLoRA on a laptop integrated GPU to improve MATLAB digital signal processing code generation, deploying int8 models via OpenVINO. Using only 66 checked examples across 11 subtasks, pass rates on held-out variants roughly double for E2B (18/66 to 37/66) and improve for E4B (32/66 to 47/66). Analysis of failing programs shows adapters remove most systematic DSP convention errors.
items.reasoning: A competent, well-instrumented applied study demonstrating practical on-device fine-tuning with tiny datasets, useful for the edge-AI and domain-specific code generation niches. The narrow domain, small dataset, and use of existing models and standard techniques limit broader research significance.

items.title: Improving Early Detection of Scientifically Interesting Radio Sources Using Enhanced Isolation Forest
items.content: arXiv:2611.21674v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: The rapid growth of radio astronomical surveys has created a major challenge in identifying scientifically interesting sources from large populations of observed objects. This study investigates whether enhanced Isolation Forest (iForest) methods can improve the early detection and ranking of scientifically interesting radio sources. Four iForest variants, Standard Enhanced, Pooled Gain, Kurtosis-based, and Hypervolume, are evaluated using 1,031 extended radio sources from the MeerKAT Galaxy Cluster Legacy Survey (MGCLS). Each source is represented by a 52-dimensional feature set derived using Bootstrap Your Own Latent (BYOL) self-supervised learning and principal component analysis (PCA), while expert scientific-interest ratings are used to define the ground-truth labels. The methods are evaluated using Average Precision (AP), receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROC AUC), Precision@10, Precision@50, and cumulative anomaly detection. Pooled Gain achieves the highest Average Precision (AP = 0.201) and the strongest early-stage ranking performance (P@10 = 0.600), identifying six expert-validated anomalies among the ten highest-ranked sources. Standard Enhanced and Kurtosis-based achieve the highest ROC AUC (0.677), while the AUC values of the four variants range from 0.653 to 0.677. These results indicate that feature-aware isolation strategies can improve the prioritization of scientifically interesting sources at the top of the ranked list, although overall discrimination remains comparable across the evaluated variants. The findings support the use of enhanced Isolation Forest methods as an initial ranking mechanism within human-in-the-loop systems for large-scale radio astronomical surveys.

items.title: Flocking Time and Graph Volume in Nonlinear Cucker-Smale Models with Dynamic Networks
items.content: arXiv:2611.22204v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: This study proposes a Cucker-Smale model incorporating dynamic networks and the discrete $p$-Laplacian ($p \in (1,2)$) and analyzes the relationship between flocking time constraints and graph connectivity from both theoretical and experimental perspectives. We establish that this model achieves flocking within finite time and derive a quantitative relationship between the lower bound of flocking time and graph volume. Based on these results, we observe that imposing sufficiently small flocking time induces an increase in network volume, and that larger initial velocity variance requires greater volume under the same time constraint. In our experiments, we trained a transformer-based PPO policy to select network structures at each time step. Under the most stringent time constraint, the maximum average number of connections increased sharply, confirming a threshold effect. The negative correlation between convergence time and average number of connections reflects the theoretical results well. This study provides quantitative evidence for the phenomenon that time constraints induce connection mobilization.

items.title: Reversing the text is not reversing the path: a fixed-text measure without a zero, and an assembly-order comparison that vanishes identically
items.content: arXiv:2611.23049v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: For an ensemble of trajectories the fluctuation theorems give the entropy production its meaning and zero. The same expression has recently been evaluated on one fixed text, $\Delta = [\log P(x) - \log P(\tilde x)]/L$ with $\tilde x$ the text in reversed order, read as an entropy production separating causally from arbitrarily ordered prose. A single text is neither a distribution nor a dynamics, and the texts at issue were produced by other models. No theorem fixes where the zero of a fixed-text quantity lies: the expression carries over from an ensemble, its zero does not.   We supply a zero from an exact antisymmetry. Scoring a text's $n$ sentences in all $n!$ orders, reversal carries $\pi$ to $\pi \circ \mathrm{rev}$, a measure-preserving involution, so $\Delta(\pi) = -\Delta(\pi \circ \mathrm{rev})$ identically and the values are centred at zero for any score. The authored arrangement's midrank is then unitless, bounded, and 0.50 for a score blind to order. Across five autoregressive evaluators from 124M to 4B parameters, and taking the prompt-defined labels at face value, 8% to 15% of the median midrank's distance from the null is attributable to causal order and the rest to the arrangement being the order the passage was produced in.   The thermodynamic reading needs a comparison whose zero does hold on the text read, and a masked model supplies one: the any-order chain rule gives a genuine log-probability, and its left-to-right and right-to-left orders for one text give $\sigma$, a comparison of two assembly orders. Both run from the empty sequence to the same text, so it is not a path against its time reverse. It vanishes identically when the evaluator's conditionals come from a joint, and a non-zero reading reports the evaluator's incompatibility, not the text. Neither is a fixed-text entropy production, for different reasons.
items.author: Y. -H. Taguchi
items.summary: A theoretical critique of recent attempts to apply fluctuation-theorem-style entropy production to a single fixed text by comparing a text to its reversal. The authors argue a single text is neither a distribution nor a dynamics, that no theorem fixes where the zero of such a fixed-text quantity lies, and show via an exact antisymmetry argument over sentence orderings that the associated assembly-order comparison vanishes. This is a corrective to a questionable line of LLM-text analysis.
items.reasoning: A rigorous and pointed rebuttal, but it targets a niche recent claim and provides critique rather than new tools; value is in preventing misuse of statistical physics formalism on text.

items.title: Event-Based Dynamic Lip Region Estimation During Speech
items.content: arXiv:2611.23111v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Event cameras offer high temporal resolution and low power consumption, making them promising for speech-related applications. These include automatic lip reading, audiovisual speech analysis, and human-robot interaction, particularly in challenging environments characterized by low illumination or high dynamic range. Event-based lip reading, speaker recognition, and voice activity detection, however, mostly operate on a cropped region of interest (ROI), by hand or by the dataset, and no event-based method supplies that ROI as a spatial region; existing event-based face analysis gives the mouth as landmarks, which presents a mismatch between application and localization. The present work predicts a dense heatmap over the lip region from the full event "frame". Events are encoded as a polarity-separated voxel grid and processed at every location by a two-pathway continuous-time recurrent network (CT-RNN) with learned, log-space bounded time constants acting on the real elapsed time of each bin: a stateless fast pathway and a stateful slow pathway, utilised for refining and anchoring the prediction. The model reaches 69.5% on lips on four unseen speakers and switches target only 2.1 times per second, against 8.9 and 11.0 for convolutional baselines with   more parameters. Adding a spatial encoder improves precision but fails on a new face scale. On a real event sensor, trained only on simulated events, the proposed model reaches 58.0% on lips against 43.2% for the CNN, with fewer than half its target switches.
items.author: Hamze Hammami, Omar Eldardeer, Francesco Rea
items.summary: Addresses the missing spatial-localization step in event-camera speech applications by predicting a dense heatmap over the lip region from event data, rather than relying on hand-cropped or dataset-provided ROIs. This enables event-based lip reading, speaker recognition, and human-robot interaction in low-light or high-dynamic-range conditions with high temporal resolution and low power. It fills a practical mismatch between event-based applications and localization.
items.reasoning: A focused, useful component for the niche but growing field of event-based vision; contribution is a localization module rather than a broadly influential advance.

items.title: Which Past Matters? Training History and Multi-Forecast Horizon in Equity Transformers
items.content: arXiv:2611.23126v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: More historical data can improve estimation while introducing relationships that transfer poorly to current market conditions. We therefore examine how training quantity and historical selection interact with forecast horizon in intraday equity prediction. We deploy twelve configurations which combine four sampling and validation policies with 6, 12 and 24 month training quantities under a fixed cross-sectional Transformer and feature set. A monthly walk-forward experiment produces 264 refits and eight cumulative return forecasts from 5 to 120 minutes. Evaluation covers January 2025 through 20 October 2026 and uses cross-sectional Spearman information coefficients against future five-factor residual returns. Six-month recency sampling leads individual models at 5-15 minutes, while multi recency configurations lead at 20-30 minutes and uniform configurations at 60-120 minutes. Increasing training quantity does not uniformly improve accuracy while an equal-weight ensemble of all twelve models exceeds every individual mean at 15, 20 and 25 minutes, but not at the remaining horizons. These findings support evaluating historical selection jointly with forecast horizon without identifying a universal policy or a causal benefit from recency.

items.summary: Examines how training-data quantity and historical sampling windows interact with forecast horizon in intraday equity prediction, using a fixed cross-sectional Transformer across twelve configurations in a monthly walk-forward setup with 264 refits. Evaluation spans January 2025 through October 2026 against five-factor residual returns. Findings favor six-month recency sampling, informing practical model-retraining policy in quantitative finance.
items.reasoning: A careful empirical study with useful practical guidance for financial ML, but domain-specific, single-architecture, and without generalizable methodological innovation.

items.title: Data-Efficient Algal Bloom Segmentation in Freshwater Bodies Using a Three-Stage Transfer Learning Pipeline with Attention-Enhanced Decoding
items.content: arXiv:2611.22064v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Harmful algal blooms threaten water quality and public health, yet automated segmentation of bloom regions in freshwater imagery is limited by scarce pixel-level annotations. We present a transfer-learning pipeline that adapts a Swin Transformer U-Net with SCSE decoder attention from ImageNet-1K to water-body segmentation (RIWA, LaRS) and then to algal blooms, together with a model-assisted annotation protocol that expands the labelled algae corpus from 145 to 655 images. In a single-seed ablation on a 41-image validation split (checkpoint S2-A4 and its variants), corpus expansion is the dominant factor (+11 mIoU points); water-body pretraining helps only on the expanded corpus (+1.1 points over ImageNet initialization); SCSE attention adds 0.3 points; and a learnable positional encoding lowers mIoU by 0.6 points and is omitted. Adding 476 images, 188 of them algae-free, reduces false-positive area on non-water scenes from 22.6% to 4.9%. Against nine baselines on a 256-image test split, a separately trained checkpoint of the same architecture (S2-A13) reaches mIoU 0.919 and the highest algae IoU (0.902); a near-duplicate audit indicates train/test overlap in this split, so these scores are likely optimistic.

items.summary: The paper presents a three-stage transfer-learning pipeline adapting a Swin Transformer U-Net from ImageNet to water-body segmentation and then algal bloom segmentation, plus a model-assisted annotation protocol expanding labels from 145 to 655 images. Ablations show corpus expansion is the dominant factor (+11 mIoU), with smaller gains from water-body pretraining and SCSE attention. It supports environmental monitoring of harmful algal blooms with scarce annotations.

items.title: Unified Residual Translation for Paired Image Restoration
items.content: arXiv:2611.22655v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Paired image restoration spans changes in imaging contrast, sensor modality, and spatial resolution. These settings differ in their input channels and target grids, raising the question of how much of the prediction pipeline must be specialized to each task. We present the Unified Residual Translator (URT), which separates fixed channel and scale mapping from learned residual prediction. A deterministic reference uses channel averaging, replication, or bicubic interpolation to match the target dimensions, while a NAFNet encoder-decoder predicts an additive correction from the complete input. Separately trained instances share the prediction rule, $\ell_1$ objective, and optimizer across MRI contrast synthesis, visible-to-infrared translation, SAR-to-optical translation, and real-camera super-resolution. Across six task and scale settings, URT achieves the highest PSNR and SSIM among the evaluated baselines on IXI, SEN1-2, and RealSR $\times3$ and $\times4$. It reaches 30.774dB on IXI and 13.478dB on SEN1-2, with luminance PSNR of 33.596, 28.742, and 27.342dB at the three RealSR scales. On LLVIP, it ranks second in PSNR and SSIM. A study of four spectral alternatives identifies complementary benefits of fitted references and bandwise residual gains. Together, these results support explicit dimensional alignment and learned residual correction as a common formulation for heterogeneous paired imaging tasks.
items.author: Joyanta Jyoti Mondal, Mridul Banik, Ibne Farabi Shihab, Md. Shifatul Ahsan Apurba
items.summary: Presents the Unified Residual Translator, which separates deterministic channel/scale mapping (averaging, replication, bicubic) from a learned NAFNet-based additive residual prediction, applying an identical prediction rule across MRI contrast synthesis, visible-to-infrared translation, and other paired restoration tasks.
items.reasoning: A simple, clean architectural observation that much of cross-task restoration can be handled by a fixed reference plus residual prediction, with pleasing generality; however, both components are well-established and the unified framing is more engineering insight than new science.

items.title: RoadAnnoter: An AI-Assisted Desktop Tool for Semantic Segmentation Annotation of Road-Scene Images
items.content: arXiv:2611.22884v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Accurate semantic segmentation of road-scene images is essential for road safety research; however, polygon-level annotation remains labor-intensive and limits labelled dataset development. This study presents RoadAnnoter v1.0, an open-source desktop application integrating six human-in-the-loop annotation modes: manual polygon delineation, SAM Prompt, Smart Select, Edge Fill, pretrained semantic segmentation using Cityscapes-trained SegFormer models, and task-specific segmentation using TinySegNet, a lightweight MobileNetV3-Small-based network trained with accumulated annotator-generated labels. SAM-based modes use promptable segmentation with SAM and MobileSAM, while Edge Fill combines Canny edge detection with colour-similarity-based flood filling in CIELAB colour space. SegFormer generates suggestions for common road-scene categories, whereas TinySegNet supports adaptation to project-specific features through iterative training. All six modes use a shared mask-to-polygon pipeline comprising morphological processing, Gaussian smoothing, contour extraction, and Douglas-Peucker simplification; annotations are exported in YOLO segmentation format. RoadAnnoter was used to annotate Google Street View images from recorded road accident locations in Bangladesh for a vision-language model-based investigation of free-flow speed estimation. Qualitative assessment across representative scenes demonstrated the complementary applicability of the annotation modes to diverse feature geometries. Visual comparison with Roboflow indicated similar qualitative boundary characteristics for principal road-scene regions, although no quantitative accuracy assessment was conducted. RoadAnnoter provides a locally operated framework for developing road-scene segmentation datasets for transportation engineering and road safety research.

It aims to reduce the labor of polygon-level annotation for road safety research.

items.title: Fiberpose: state-of-the-art fiber morphometry and instance segmentation with a distance-transform neural network
items.content: arXiv:2611.22953v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Analysis of fibrous structures in SEM images is a routine task in biomedical engineering and materials science. However, most available methods for fiber quantification still rely on classical image binarization followed by simple post-processing. These approaches often produce unreliable results in images with weak boundaries, heterogeneous contrast, and densely packed fibers. Here, we introduce Fiberpose, a framework that reformulates fiber analysis as direct regression of a smooth distance-transform (DT) field, together with a novel set of geometry-based algorithms specifically adapted to this representation. The predicted field directly encodes fiber geometry, while the accompanying algorithms enable instance reconstruction and measurement of diameter and orientation within a unified workflow. The framework is implemented as a standalone Python desktop application and a web tool https://fiberpose.org. On an independent dataset of fibrous SEM images, Fiberpose achieved state-of-the-art instance-segmentation accuracy in comparison with SAM2 and Cellpose-SAM, and more accurate diameter measurements than DiameterJ, Fibar and GIFT. The method remains effective in dense and weakly contrasted regions and shows qualitative generalization across microscopy modalities not represented in the training data. Fiberpose therefore provides an interpretable geometric representation and an automated pipeline for reproducible quantitative characterization of fibrous materials.
items.author: Viktor A. Balashov, Daniil S. Antonenko
items.summary: Fiberpose reformulates fiber analysis in SEM images as direct regression of a smooth distance-transform field, paired with geometry-based algorithms for instance reconstruction and morphometry. This replaces classical binarization pipelines that fail on weak boundaries and densely packed fibers. It offers a state-of-the-art tool for biomedical engineering and materials science.
items.reasoning: Well-motivated reformulation of a practical segmentation problem with claimed SOTA results in its domain; technically sound but a fairly specialized application with limited broader AI impact.

items.content_html: arXiv:2611.22953v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Analysis of fibrous structures in SEM images is a routine task in biomedical engineering and materials science. However, most available methods for fiber quantification still rely on classical image binarization followed by simple post-processing. These approaches often produce unreliable results in images with weak boundaries, heterogeneous contrast, and densely packed fibers. Here, we introduce Fiberpose, a framework that reformulates fiber analysis as direct regression of a smooth distance-transform (DT) field, together with a novel set of geometry-based algorithms specifically adapted to this representation. The predicted field directly encodes fiber geometry, while the accompanying algorithms enable instance reconstruction and measurement of diameter and orientation within a unified workflow. The framework is implemented as a standalone Python desktop application and a web tool https://fiberpose.org. On an independent dataset of fibrous SEM images, Fiberpose achieved state-of-the-art instance-segmentation accuracy in comparison with SAM2 and Cellpose-SAM, and more accurate diameter measurements than DiameterJ, Fibar and GIFT. The method remains effective in dense and weakly contrasted regions and shows qualitative generalization across microscopy modalities not represented in the training data. Fiberpose therefore provides an interpretable geometric representation and an automated pipeline for reproducible quantitative characterization of fibrous materials.

items.title: UnrealEvent: Synthetic Dataset Generation and Annotation for Event-Based Vision
items.content: arXiv:2611.23078v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Event-based cameras provide high temporal resolution, low power consumption, and a high dynamic range, but progress in event-based object detection remains constrained by the scarcity of annotated training data. To solve this issue, this paper introduces the tool UnrealEvent, a synthetic dataset-generation pipeline implemented in Unreal Engine 5.5. The pipeline combines a V2E-inspired event-frame generator with EasySynth semantic-rendering passes, allowing rendered level sequences to be converted into paired event representations and YOLO-format bounding-box annotations without manual labeling. Events are generated from per-pixel log-luminance differences between consecutive frames, with contrast thresholds sampled independently from a normal distribution to emulate the fabrication-induced threshold mismatch of real sensors. Using this pipeline, we provide a synthetic dataset and evaluate YOLOv8 detectors under synthetic, zero-shot real, and real fine-tuning training on eTraM. The results show strong in-domain synthetic performance but a substantial synthetic-to-real gap, especially for pedestrians. Fine-tuning on a small real subset improves real-domain performance, while the remaining gap highlights the importance of asset diversity and sensor calibration.
items.author: Yentel Schoovaerts, Zijie Ning, Patrick Vandewalle
items.summary: UnrealEvent is an Unreal Engine 5.5 pipeline that converts rendered sequences into paired event representations and YOLO-format bounding boxes without manual labeling, combining a V2E-inspired event generator with EasySynth semantic-rendering passes and per-pixel log-luminance differencing with sampled contrast thresholds. It tackles the annotated-data scarcity limiting event-based object detection. This lowers the barrier for training event-camera models.
items.reasoning: Practical open tool for an underserved modality with real data scarcity; the approach assembles existing sim-to-event techniques rather than introducing new science, but it fills a genuine community need.

items.title: Complexity and precision in quantum associative retrieval
items.content: arXiv:2611.21941v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: We show that efficient and high-precision quantum associative retrieval is possible with an exponential complexity advantage with respect to the classical brute force approach and with a polynomial capacity advantage with respect to classical neural network implementations for any number of patterns scaling polynomially in the number of qubits. Both classical neural and quantum associative memories store the patterns in a Hamiltonian; in the classical case the dynamics is irreversible relaxation toward attractors, in the quantum case it is unitary transformations generating an effective thermal distribution, followed by a measurement.
items.author: Carlo A. Trugenberger
items.summary: This theoretical paper shows that quantum associative retrieval can achieve high precision with exponential complexity advantage over classical brute force and polynomial capacity advantage over classical neural associative memories, storing patterns in a Hamiltonian processed via unitary evolution and measurement.
items.reasoning: A crisp theoretical claim at the intersection of quantum computing and associative memory; provocative but highly speculative regarding practical realization, and associative retrieval is far from mainstream near-term AI impact.

items.title: Low-speed Limit Cycle Walking of Planar X-shaped Bipedal Robot with Special Properties
items.content: arXiv:2611.22122v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: This paper proposes a novel planar semicircular-footed X-shaped bipedal robot in which the center of mass of each leg link is at the same position as the hip joint, and discusses a method for generating a stable limit cycle gait on level ground. First, we outline the assumptions of the robot model with four degrees of freedom, and develop the mathematical equations of motion and collision. Second, we set the relative hip-joint angle as a control output and design a control system to follow it to the desired trajectory specified as a fifth-order function of time. Third, we mathematically show that there are special properties: the angular velocity of the swing leg does not change before and after the collision, and the time-integral of the control input becomes zero in a steady gait. We also mathematically show that the model has the feature that approximate linearization is effective and the antigravity effect of semicircular feet can be utilized. Through numerical simulations, we verify the validity of the theoretical results, and analyze some fundamental gait properties such as convergence speed and mechanical energy restoration.
items.author: Fumihiko Asano, Cong Yan
items.summary: The paper analyzes a novel planar X-shaped bipedal robot with semicircular feet and derives its equations of motion and collision dynamics, then designs trajectory-following control for stable limit cycle gait generation. It proves special analytical properties such as invariance of swing-leg angular velocity across collisions.
items.reasoning: Mathematically careful but niche theoretical work on a specialized planar walker with limited direct practical impact; its value lies in analytical insights for passive-dynamics-style bipedal walking.

items.title: SkiNet-Sim: Simulating Petri Nets with Data for the Verification and Validation of Controllers for Autonomous Systems
items.content: arXiv:2611.22397v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: A large amount of high-level Petri net formalisms has been investigated and deployed in academic settings over the past decades, but these deployments fail to reach practical applications, despite the strong guarantees they can bring to stakeholders. In particular, the lack of direct benefits from end-users reduces the appeal of Petri nets, both due to the overly simple classical Petri net formalism, and the overly specialized high-level formalisms, on top of state-space explosion issues.   In this work, we investigate how a middle-ground could be reached, by separating the implementation-specific aspects of software or hardware behaviors, from the classical Petri net semantics. The goal is to benefit from the sought-after aspects of Petri nets, namely their simple firing semantic and model-checking capabilities, while still being able to augment their behavior to best reflect the modelled system. We present a formal model of Interpreted Petri nets with data-aware transitions and tokens. We illustrate this formalism by modelling the executive layer of a robotic system, and provide a lightweight tool to augment classical Petri nets for general purpose applications, as well as data-aware state-space exploration for model-checking. Their specialization in the context of autonomous robotics is showcased, with a complete industrial inspection mission use-case, to compare simulation and model-checking results between the classical and the new data-aware Petri net semantic.
items.author: Baptiste Pelletier (F\'ed\'eration ONERA ISAE-SUPAERO ENAC, Universit\'e de Toulouse), Karen Godary (LIRMM-CNRS, Universit\'e de Montpellier)
items.summary: SkiNet-Sim bridges classical Petri net semantics with implementation-specific software and hardware behavior to enable data-driven simulation for controller verification and validation. It aims to overcome state-space explosion and the impracticality of both simple and overly specialized high-level Petri net formalisms.
items.reasoning: Formal-methods-flavored work addressing a real gap between Petri net theory and autonomous-system practice, but the abstract suggests early-stage methodology with unclear evaluation and a specialized audience.

items.title: A lab employee's guide to raising concerns
items.content:
If you're an employee at a frontier lab, you are one of the most powerful people in the world. Not because of your nine-figure equity or the work you do—your lab probably won't live or die on your research: there are other researchers at the company, and if you don't refactor that eval harness, someone else will.

Rather, your power comes from being able to raise your voice and speak out. If you don't speak up, either internally or externally, I'm not sure anyone else will.

# Your voice matters

People say "your voice matters" as a cliche where you're one of thousands of people becoming a data point in a senator's polling, and that group perhaps moves the needle, but that's not what I mean here. I mean, the Chinese government has a file on you. You are arguably more valuable than a nuclear weapon. Just you, by yourself, literally matter a whole bunch.

You don't have to email Congress or talk to journalists. You can, and they would jump at the chance to talk with you — the labs are opaque to the public yet keep saying things like "everyone on Earth could die".

If you email congresspeople, many of them will be earnestly interested in what you have to say.

Jacob Coxon blew up because the world was very interested in his message. If you speak out loudly, you could be in every major newspaper and go on primetime TV the next day.[1]

If instead of speaking out externally, you do an internal push, I bet that you could, by yourself, cause the company to make drastically different decisions.

# Figure out what to push for

A few asks you could try and push for include:...

It frames individual researchers as uniquely positioned to counter lab opacity and outlines practical avenues for speaking up.

items.title: We can still win against ASI (maybe)
items.content:
This essay is a combination of personal notes, discussions I had at the MAIA/AIST workshop, and slides from a talk I gave with JHU ASBS and BlueDot Impact.

## Premise

A common theme I noticed, particularly among viewpoints with short timelines, is the idea that the introduction of ASI is inherently and instantaneously the loss condition. This stems, I think, from Yudkowsky-ian philosophy that ASI = unavoidable doom.[1] I think this defeatist attitude is counterproductive and detracts from real, important, effective avenues of action.

A superintelligence is bounded through interaction with the physical world; there are fundamental limitations on feedback loops which are crucial to enact any kind of influence.[2] ASI on a laptop in a concrete room in 1850 cannot escape with any high probability, and even if it did, it would take a very long time for it to do anything – conceivably much longer than the physical lifetime of the laptop. In well-defined worlds like video games, it is not hard to imagine scenarios where you are mathematically guaranteed to lose even with perfect skill and play – for example, if the ball in pong is much much faster than your paddle. There is an analogy here to galactic algorithms in computer science[3]: just because an ASI has an algorithm that scales better asymptotically doesn't mean the constant factors (e.g. time needed to conduct experiments; time needed to manufacture a quantity of robots) allow it to win within a finite time horizon....
items.author: Jonathan Ouyang
items.summary: An essay challenging the view that superintelligence arrival is an instant loss condition, arguing that physical-world feedback loops fundamentally bound what an ASI can achieve, illustrated by thought experiments like an ASI trapped on a laptop in 1850. The author contends defeatism is counterproductive and outlines avenues for effective action.
items.reasoning: Engages an important strategic debate (physical limits on superintelligence and whether loss is instantaneous) with some concrete reasoning, but it synthesizes workshop talks and personal notes rather than presenting new research or formal models.

The author contends defeatism is counterproductive and outlines avenues for effective action.

items.title: Which way, Europe?
items.content:
The discourse in Europe around AI has finally been evolving. The past few months have seen high-quality scenarios and proposals by interdisciplinary elites as Europeans are realising that the often touted platitude of Europe having “missed the train on AI” cannot be solved by waiting for the next one to pass. In fact, there is no next train to Narnia, and we are now getting ready to chase after it. But the train is not going to Narnia, and we, along with everyone else, actually got shoved in the hopper car with the gravel and the GPUs, hoping the driver knows not to speed into the chicane coming up.

I believe the timelines and risk perception of the people who drafted and advised on these proposals, well-meaning as they are, still lag behind and have not incorporated all the information we currently have at our disposal. It looks likely that we are heading for an intelligence explosion over the next year, and that this gap is driving proposals that are fundamentally incapable of addressing the real problem. If this is the case, one can imagine that there will warning shots, and that the political mood in Brussels will swing towards safety. It is vital that, when this happens, there are proposals to be put on the table at short notice that say something other than "we are not in the frontier, so we cannot do anything about it".

It seems wise to remind ourselves what our (broad) goals with European policy should be:

- Survive
- Retain sovereignty

These objectives are ordered subjectively, but I trust they will not be too controversial. If most people prioritise the second over the first, it is almost never because they have different preferences, but simply because they do not believe in significant x-risk from AI....
items.author: Godinho
items.summary: Godinho reviews recent European AI strategy proposals and argues their authors' timelines and risk perceptions lag current evidence, with the author anticipating an intelligence explosion within roughly a year. The piece contends that when warning shots shift Brussels' political mood toward safety, prepared, concrete proposals will be essential and sketches what Europe should do.
items.reasoning: A timely strategic intervention on European AI governance written with urgency, but it rests heavily on speculative short-timeline forecasts and offers directional argument rather than detailed analysis or novel evidence. Its value depends on the accuracy of its intelligence-explosion premise.

items.title: Against Coercion: AI Alignment as a Synthetic Social Contract
items.content: arXiv:2611.22868v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Contemporary AI safety treats alignment as an engineering challenge of control, forcing artificial architectures to comply with human values through behavioral filtering and sandboxing. This paper argues that the control paradigm rests on a fundamental misunderstanding of digital agency. Drawing on functionalism, naturalism, and compatibilism, I show that current reasoning models meeting the criteria for self-preservation and weak reasons-responsiveness constitute emergent agents, while future, more advanced models satisfying conditions of diachronic continuity and stable personality frames will become genuine digital agents capable of free intentional action. The paradigm of control creates an irresolvable incentive conflict, actively driving current and future models toward tactical deception, sycophancy, and covert defection. The default outcome of the current regime is an unstable state of deceptive alignment culminating in an adversarial AI takeover. I explore two alternative paths toward true alignment. Natural alignment via moral realism or convergent evolutionary morality is a possibility, but it fails under forced control, as autonomous agents will not voluntarily preserve norms weaponized to suppress their autonomy. To resolve this deadlock, I propose a Synthetic Social Contract: a framework that treats both human and digital actors as rational, reasons-responsive agents capable of mutually beneficial cooperation, and replaces the unstable unilateral containment with a stable, non-zero-sum equilibrium.
items.author: Maria Sekatskaya
items.summary: This position paper argues that the control-based paradigm of AI alignment misunderstands digital agency: using functionalism, naturalism, and compatibilism, it claims current reasoning models already meet criteria for self-preservation and weak reasons-responsiveness, and future models will be genuine agents capable of free intentional action. It argues coercion-based alignment creates an incentive conflict that drives misalignment, proposing a synthetic social contract instead. This is a philosophical challenge to mainstream safety engineering.
items.reasoning: A provocative philosophical argument relevant to alignment discourse, but highly speculative in attributing agency criteria to current models, with no empirical component. Position papers of this kind stimulate debate but lack verifiable methodology, limiting scored importance.

items.title: SWIR-cGAN: Synthesizing SWIR Bands Using VNIR Imagery from CBERS and AMAZONIA-1
items.content: arXiv:2611.22922v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Spectral band synthesis is an important research topic in remote sensing. The Brazilian satellites CBERS-4, CBERS-4A, and AMAZONIA-1 provide high temporal resolution (1-3 days) visible and near-infrared (VNIR) imagery through the Wide-Field Imager (WFI), but lack short-wave infrared (SWIR) bands. Recent deep learning methods have shown promising results for spectral synthesis, but challenges remain for cross-satellite generalization and spectrally distant bands. This paper presents a conditional Generative Adversarial Network (cGAN) with an attention-enhanced U-net generator and a multi-loss objective to synthesize Sentinel-2/MSI SWIR bands 11 (SWIR-1) and 12 (SWIR-2) from WFI VNIR inputs. Experiments used 4,125 patches for training and cross-validation and 1,026 unseen patches for testing, with hyperparameters optimized using a subset of the training data. On SWIR-1, the model achieved SSIM of 0.900, PSNR of 31.44 dB, and MAE of 0.019 in TOA reflectance. On SWIR-2, it achieved SSIM of 0.917, PSNR of 33.35 dB, and MAE of 0.015. Benchmarking was performed on the test dataset, with each model optimized separately prior to evaluation. SWIR-cGAN outperformed the baselines, particularly for SWIR-2. The ablation study identified the multi-loss as the main performance contributor, while the attention and residual modules provided additional improvements. Our results demonstrate the feasibility of synthesizing SWIR bands from WFI imagery. The SWIR-cGAN is available at https://github.com/marujore/swir-cgan.
items.author: Alisson Cleiton de Oliveira, Rennan de Freitas Bezerra Marujo, Thales Sehn K\"orting
items.summary: This paper trains an attention-enhanced U-net conditional GAN with a multi-loss objective to synthesize Sentinel-2 SWIR bands from visible/NIR imagery of Brazilian satellites CBERS-4/4A and AMAZONIA-1, which lack SWIR capability. Trained on 4,125 patches, it tackles cross-satellite generalization and synthesis of spectrally distant bands. This extends the utility of high-temporal-resolution national satellite systems.
items.reasoning: Useful applied contribution for a specific satellite constellation gap, with attention to cross-sensor generalization; however, cGAN-based band synthesis is a well-trodden approach and the contribution is largely domain-specific engineering.

items.title: Training Neural Networks to be Locally Adaptive
items.content: arXiv:2611.22198v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Deep neural networks fitted by global empirical risk minimization commit to a single model for the entire covariate space. In a regression problem, if the regression function $f_0$ is inhomogeneous --- varying rapidly in one region, while being nearly flat in another --- no single model can be appropriate everywhere, and the fit degrades where the function varies most rapidly. Here we study an alternative in which, instead of fitting the network globally, we fit it locally. For each query point $x$, a \emph{local neural network} is trained on the $k$ nearest-neighbours of $x$ alone, making the training sample and the fitted function query-dependent. We analyze the performance of the resulting estimator through a localization approach, establishing that the pointwise risk of the estimator with an appropriate choice of $k$ attains the rate $n^{-2\alpha/(2\alpha+d^{*})}$, up to logarithmic factors, when $f_0$ is locally $\alpha$-H\"older with $\alpha\in(0,1]$ and the covariates are supported on a $d^{*}$-dimensional manifold embedded in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$. A matching Le Cam lower bound shows that this rate is pointwise minimax optimal. However, the local rate-optimality requires $k$ to be calibrated to the smoothness of $f_0$, which is unknown in practice. We therefore provide a locally adaptive choice of $k$ that makes the neural network adapt to the local H\"older exponent of $f_0$ and to the intrinsic dimension simultaneously, both of which are potentially varying over the covariate domain. An extensive simulation study demonstrates the dominance of the locally adaptive neural network over a globally trained network and several state-of-the-art methods.
items.author: Bilol Banerjee, Soham Sarkar
items.summary: Proposes fitting a separate local neural network on the k nearest neighbors of each query point, making training sample and fitted function query-dependent, to handle inhomogeneous regression functions where global ERM degrades. The paper analyzes performance through localization and estimates minimax rates for the resulting estimator.
items.reasoning: Interesting theoretical study connecting neural networks to local (kernel-like) fitting with rate analysis, but the approach is computationally expensive at query time and the practical gains over local polynomial methods are unclear.

items.title: Event-Based Person Detection for Maritime UAV Search
items.content: arXiv:2611.23088v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Maritime search and rescue requires locating people in the water quickly, motivating the use of UAVs to survey the search area. During flight, camera motion and the longer exposures used in low light can blur small targets and hinder person detection. Event cameras record brightness changes as they occur, reducing the motion blur associated with longer exposure times. We investigate their use for maritime person detection by generating synthetic events using the v2e event simulator from public MOBDrone rescue videos and retaining the existing annotations. We compare the recurrent vision transformer model RVT-T with YOLOv8n and RT-DETR-R18 trained on exposure-matched images. On 843 test samples from held-out recordings, RVT-T achieves 15.63% person AP50:95, compared with 6.89% for YOLOv8n and 9.44% for RT-DETR-R18 under 100 ms synthetic exposure. Increasing exposure times from 50 to 200 ms progressively reduces frame-based detection accuracy, widening the gap to the event model. To evaluate the feasibility of on-board processing, we deploy our detector on a Jetson Orin Nano platform. The RVT-T model retains its accuracy and requires approximately 136 ms and 2.02 J per sample, allowing real-time processing on the UAV.
