items.title: The Natural Alliance of Everyone Else
items.content:
Alignment as the foundation

Listen to this post on the Non-Zero-Sum James podcast

We've been on a long safari through the various collective crises we face as a world together—and it paints an admittedly bleak picture, but there is light at the end of this tunnel—after all, we all want this to succeed, right? Do you know anyone who wants humanity to fail? If 8 billion intelligent people, and untold billions of intelligent AIs, want to keep playing this game, surely there's a way.

Or a silent rogue, building their skills in secret to unleash vigilante justice on a crime-ridden underworld. Heroic narratives often focus on an extraordinary individual, a superman, a wonder woman, who is singularly powerful. But, inevitably they find themselves facing an equal or greater power in the form of their nemesis, and there's a great deal of symmetry in this archetypal relationship. So, what is the difference between this hero and their nemesis?

Is it merely an arbitrary competition between two powers, the result of which only serves to place ultimate power in the hands of one or the other?

"No."

There is an important difference between a good-guy and a bad-guy. Inevitably the bad-guy is playing for ultimate power and subjugation of the world to their will—they are looking to win the game, and to do so, everyone else must lose—a zero-sum game. The good-guy is playing for something different, usually to "restore balance" in one form or another. They are fighting, not to win the game, but to allow the game to continue, they are playing a non-zero-sum game, an infinite game where the goal is not to determine the future for everyone, but to allow for individuals to determine their own futures. This win doesn't see unity and freedom as mutually exclusive, but rather as complementary.

Well, that's how I see it anyway....
items.author: James Stephen Brown
items.summary: A wide-ranging philosophical essay arguing that humanity and most AI systems share a natural alliance because both want the game of civilization to continue, contrasting heroic archetypes with their nemeses to explore what distinguishes good actors from bad. It attempts to ground an optimistic collective-security framing for coexistence with AI.
items.reasoning: Speculative and abstract essay writing with podcast promotion; lacks technical content, formal argument, or empirical grounding. Low research value despite an interesting core intuition about broad-based coalitions.

items.title: Read More Facts and Fewer Theories
items.content:
I’m a broken record on this, but almost all of the most ~thoughtful~ people I know (or have interviewed) have memorized a lot of dates, places, names, numbers etc. And not just memorized, but care about their ability to recall specifics.

Seek truth from facts. It’s the only way. — Joe Wiesenthal

So many people reason through heuristics, like who is aligned with whom, what personal financial interests they might have at stake, what peer group pressure they get. And I get it, because these things are complicated.

But the way out, as always, is to seek truth from facts. — Joe Wiesenthal

“You open the newspaper to an article on some subject you know well. In [Murray Gell-Mann’s] case, physics. In mine, show business. You read the article and see the journalist has absolutely no understanding of either the facts or the issues. … [Then you] turn the page to national or international affairs, and read with renewed interest as if the rest of the newspaper was somehow more accurate about far-off Palestine than it was about the story you just read. You turn the page, and forget what you know.” — Michael Crichton

Many who read about Diamond’s geographic determinism, Fukuyama’s end of history, Morris’s energy-capture thesis, Acemoglu and Robinson’s inclusive and extractive institutions, or Turchin’s structural-demographic theory would have been better served learning basic empirical facts about historical or present societies.

There are a bunch of reasons:...

items.title: Empirical feelings
items.content:
I often talk about feelings that I purportedly feel. ’That was fun!’, ‘I’m so glad this happened’, ‘I am overcome by sadness’. But a few years ago, in one of those discussions about transforming the known universe into optimal happiness substrate, it came to my attention that I didn’t really know what I was talking about with things like that.

For one thing, I just wasn’t sure I knew what, for instance, anger characteristically felt like (in my defense, I’m usually distracted by some incredibly annoying thing happening whenever I am experiencing it). I could probably recognize anger, and was probably talking about it accurately when I said, ‘I am angry’. But if I tried to imagine anger when I wasn’t angry, I was not sure I got it right, and I didn’t have a good explicit description of it.

But aside from that—whether or not I’m on top of what the famous feelings actually feel like—there is a question of whether the feelings I have are basically the ones people usually talk about. Like, if nobody had ever mentioned any feelings, and I had to notice them myself and figure out introspectively which ones existed, would I come up with the usual list? I kind of doubted it.

So for a few weeks I tried to make a list of feelings as I experienced them, or as I particularly remembered experiencing them at other times, as if I didn’t know the usual list. And to pay attention to what they were actually like....
items.author: KatjaGrace
items.summary: A personal essay in which the author describes systematically cataloging her own introspective experiences after realizing she could not reliably identify or describe standard emotions like anger. It raises questions about whether privately noticed feelings would match the culturally standard list of emotions.
items.reasoning: Interesting introspective and philosophical musing with possible marginal relevance to consciousness debates, but it is personal narrative with no research methodology or AI-specific content.

It raises questions about whether privately noticed feelings would match the culturally standard list of emotions.

But aside from that—whether or not I’m on top of what the famous feelings actually feel like—there is a question of whether the feelings I have are basically the ones people usually talk about. Like, if nobody had ever mentioned any feelings, and I had to notice them myself and figure out introspectively which ones existed, would I come up with the usual list? I kind of doubted it.

So for a few weeks I tried to make a list of feelings as I experienced them, or as I particularly remembered experiencing them at other times, as if I didn’t know the usual list. And to pay attention to what they were actually like....

items.title: A Beginner’s Guide to Writing Essays/Blog Posts
items.content:
Why should you bother spending time writing an essay?

Through investing many hours into writing something, you extract the swirling chaos of ideas from your mind and bring order to them. The result? You come to understand something on a much deeper level, and can even experience long-term changes in your behavior.

I’ve been writing essays for three years now, and at first it was terribly difficult. But over the years, I developed a writing method that makes it easy to get started, maintain motivation, and finish an essay.

- Put away all technology. No computers or phones. Don’t even wear a watch, either, because knowing the time can put psychological pressure on yourself. Boredom, while it may feel uncomfortable, is your friend —your brain hates wasted space and will fill the void with creative thoughts and ideas. Instead of using technology, write with a pen and paper. Writing by hand forces you to slow down and mull on ideas for longer—this is good.
- Write down any ideas, then construct a low-effort outline. Struggling to put pen to paper? Worried about writing something nonsensical? Don’t worry! Just write any thought that pops into your head—they should be extremely rough and underdeveloped, written as a bulleted list. None of this writing will likely end up in your finished essay. Once you’ve squeezed out as many ideas as you can, it’s time to order them into an outline, which I prefer to write as another bulleted list. The outline should also be pretty low effort. You’re just linking your ideas together, and maybe adding some transitions between ideas.
- Use a second sheet of paper for the rough draft. Emphasis on rough. The first draft will likely be shit. Keep this in mind because it takes the pressure off from having to be perfect. Nobody will ever see this version. Just continue to reference your outline, to keep you organized, as you develop your thoughts further. items.title: Analyzing Learned Convnet Features with Dirichlet Process Gaussian Mixture Models
items.content: arXiv:1702.07189v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Convolutional Neural Networks (Convnets) have achieved good results in a range of computer vision tasks the recent years. Though given a lot of attention, visualizing the learned representations to interpret Convnets, still remains a challenging task. The high dimensionality of internal representations and the high abstractions of deep layers are the main challenges when visualizing Convnet functionality. We present in this paper a technique based on clustering internal Convnet representations with a Dirichlet Process Gaussian Mixture Model, for visualization of learned representations in Convnets. Our method copes with the high dimensionality of a Convnet by clustering representations across all nodes of each layer. We will discuss how this application is useful when considering transfer learning, i.e.\ transferring a model trained on one dataset to solve a task on a different one.
items.author: David Malmgren-Hansen, Allan Aasbjerg Nielsen, Rasmus Engholm
items.summary: This is a 2017-era arXiv cross-listing proposing to visualize learned Convnet representations by clustering internal layer activations with Dirichlet Process Gaussian Mixture Models, coping with high dimensionality across layer nodes. Relative to current standards, both the architecture studied and the interpretability technique are heavily superseded by modern tools.
items.reasoning: A resurfaced old paper on interpretability of CNNs, a setting far removed from the current research frontier. The method was reasonable for its time but has been overtaken by modern interpretability approaches; the cross-listing provides little new relevance for 2026 readers.

items.title: EK (emancipatory knowledge) in EA (effective altruism)
items.content:
An academic friend of mine once said something about how the knowledge she gained during her studies was emancipatory.

This feels like it could almost be a truism, but I would probably add 2 things that knowledge acquisition needs to successfully be "emancipatory".

-->coherent body of knowledge (clear how different pieces of knowledge link together)

-->practical body of knowledge (applicable to the real world as you know it)

I think the AI safety/EA communities does this exceptionally well (and maybe has a significant head-start considering the type of people that are drawn to this space(?)) while it is grossly under-looked in classical educational spaces and, I'd argue, especially STEM spaces (my bias speaking).

What should happen is: a student gets a problem and works backwards. All knowledge gained will be part of a coherent body (the problem at hand) as well as practical (the problem at hand exists in the real world).

Most classical curricula seem to be built up this way, except for the crucial fact that they miss the problem. I'd love the problem to be formulated more along the lines of:

-> Lots of people get sick

-> Some of these diseases are transmissible

-> You can use epidemiology to study the transmissible diseases

-> Modelling is an important part of epidemiology

-> Bayesian statistics are an important of this modelling

That's why you're sitting through a class of incomprehensible numbers and that, to me, makes sense.

But way too often the problem is given in an abstracted form and the pipeline ends up looking like:

-> Lots of people get sick

-> I made the decision to study biomedical sciences 3 years ago

.....

-> Bayesian statistics (???)...

items.title: Lorxus Does Budget Inkhaven For a Third Time: 11/11~11/17
items.content:
Budget Inkhaven is happening again, so I'm doing it again. As with the last two times (1, 2), I've decided to post these in weekly batches. This is the first of five; the last one will once again include a postmortem. I'm posting these here because Blogspot's comment apparatus sucks and also because no one will comment otherwise.

1. Hold Your Breath

You sacrifice a tiny bit of your life; you wait in stillness; you speedrun the katabasis and then the return to the everyday.

2. In Defense of High-Effort Food

Anyone still up for getting your hedons and utilons separately?

3. Running Up That Hill

Here's one riddle in two guises:

"Why is it sometimes so hard for me to get through my to-do list?"

and

"Why aren't flammable substances always on fire?"

4. My Least Favorite AI Alignment Plan Schemas That Still Maybe Even Work

Perhaps a quote from outside the usual canon will put poetry to the problem: "...[I]f you are looking for a Moses to lead you out of this... wilderness, you will stay right where you are. I would not lead you into the promised land if I could, because if I led you in, some one else would lead you out. You must use your heads as well as your hands, and get yourself out of your present condition...". Just so. Right; back to it, then?

5. If You Invite Me to Apply Unsolicited and Then Drop Me in an Early Round, I'm Going to Blacklist You

It's a languid Tuesday evening when the email hits your inbox. "Invitation to Apply for an Upcoming Fellowship" is the topic. You've been trying for a grant, which so far hasn't gone as hoped, so you open it. You recognize the org's name; they do good work. You think their recent paper had some flaws, but on the whole their organizational heart seems to be in the right place, and they're doing the work.

"Hello!" it begins. Your name's in the next sentence...

6. Take Heart, If You Proved A Known Result...

items.title: Two New Restaurants on Morrison Ave
items.content:
Despite being a professional food critic I rarely eat out, but when two
new restaurants opened up literally in my own house I couldn't
possibly not stay home.

These are exclusive establishments: there's no sign, no website,
and you have to know someone.  Fortunately, I go way back with both chefs.

Tables at The Tiny Restaurant ("TTR") are notoriously hard to come by,
but I snagged a 2pm reservation at 1:55pm.  TTR takes the small-plates
trend to its natural endpoint.  I was immediately impressed by the
decor; everything was indeed tiny:

The seat was a floor cushion, and while I understand there are
cultures where this is traditional, if I'd grown up in one I'd have
maintained more flexibility with age.

I ordered the "fridge-to-table" Apple Cheese Circles, and
when they arrived I was mildly surprised to notice there was nothing
circular about them: they were clearly snowflakes.

While I have nothing against snowflakes, I do like to know what I'm
getting up front.  Still, they were delicious, a classy
reinterpretation of the genre, and appropriately tiny.

The water cup was tiny as well, which does have a distinct downside:
if the waiter is not attentive, you'll spend a lot of time thirsty.
As the only patron I had no issue with service, but I do wonder what
this place is like during peak hours.

When it came time to pay, the cook emerged from the kitchen and swiped
my credit card, in the sense of "ran away cackling."  They did
eventually return the card, but only after extended negotiation.

Overall, 4/5: food and decor were good and the service was attentive
if larcenous, but the portions were tiny, and the seating uncomfortable.

My next stop was a restaurant new enough that it doesn't yet have a
name, but already bearing the prestigious "Sir Nixafur
Approved" seal:

The decor screamed "relaxed, casual, homestyle", artfully giving the
impression that the proprietor was hosting you at their own dining
room table:...
